title: Reading 1 · Empirical studies
sourceText: Reading 1: Empirical studies

title: Phonemes and letters
sourceText:
Do you remember when we discussed 
phonemes at the beginning of the semester?
What was the first thing I wanted you to 
remember about phonemes?
paragraphs: **Phonemes are speech-sound categories, not letters.** A writing system represents language, but its symbols do not have to correspond one-to-one with those categories.
A letter can contribute to different pronunciations, and a phoneme can be represented by different spellings.

title: Orthographic depth
sourceText:
We were able to demonstrate that 
phonemes are not letters, but also 
that letters are not phonemes with 
a “mispronouncing contest” in 
which people willfully 
mispronounced words like:
COLONEL
PARADIGM
We also talked about how some 
scripts (like Pinyin for Mandarin 
and French) are relatively regular.
This difference between scripts is also referred to as orthographic depth. 
English, due its irregularities is a relatively deep script. 
Finnish and Korean are very shallow scripts.
paragraphs: **Orthographic depth** describes how consistently spelling corresponds to pronunciation. English is relatively deep because many spellings do not transparently specify their sounds.
COLONEL and PARADIGM make the problem concrete. Applying common letter–sound patterns can produce a plausible-looking pronunciation that is wrong for the actual word.

In shallower writing systems, such as Finnish and Korean, spelling–sound correspondences are more predictable. The comparison concerns the writing system, not the intelligence or ability of its readers.

title: Transparent spelling in Finnish
sourceText:
Some writing systems, like Finnish, are 
very “transparent” (or “shallow” 
according to the Orthographic Depth 
Hypothesis).
Let’s listen to this beginning Finnish 
lesson and follow along with the text…
After about a minute of this, you 
probably get the idea?
Each letter corresponds more or less 
unambiguously to one phoneme. 
Doubled letters actually correspond to 
geminated consonants or long vowels.
Finnish children learn to decode
pronunciations for written forms very 
very quickly. 
http://tasteoffinnish.fi/lesson1-1/
paragraphs: **Finnish has a shallow orthography.** Letters correspond relatively unambiguously to phonemes, so learning a spelling–sound correspondence helps with many different words.
Doubled letters represent a meaningful length distinction. A doubled consonant is geminated, and a doubled vowel is long.
This regularity helps Finnish children learn decoding quickly. Decoding means generating a pronunciation from a written form, whether or not its meaning is familiar.

title: Learning to decode across languages
sourceText:
In fact, English is a bit of an outlier 
among languages that use the Roman 
alphabet. 
One result is that kids learn to decode 
more slowly in English.
In Grade 1, kids learning a wide variety 
of other languages are able to generate 
plausible pronunciations for 
“pseudowords,” (made up words that 
follow the spelling and sound patterns 
of their language) at a much higher rate 
than English learners.
paragraphs: **Pseudoword reading tests decoding.** Because a pseudoword is not a familiar stored word, the child must generalize from learned spelling–sound patterns.

The comparison involves Grade 1 children learning different alphabetic writing systems. Children learning many other languages produce plausible pseudoword pronunciations more successfully than English learners.
English's less predictable correspondences help explain why decoding develops more slowly. This task does not measure the child's entire language ability.

title: Korean letter forms and sounds
sourceText:
Korean is even more regular than 
Finnish!
The symbols for similar phonemes 
are represented as similar to one 
another. 
What orthographic feature 
corresponds roughly to velar place of 
articulation, for example?
paragraphs: **Korean writing represents sound structure systematically.** Related phonemes can have related written shapes, so the visual forms themselves reflect aspects of phonological organization.
The letters are arranged into syllable blocks with initial, medial and sometimes final positions. Those positions are not three unrelated pictures of whole words.
The velar consonant forms share the basic angular ㄱ shape. Additional strokes or doubling distinguish related consonants.

title: Pseudoword decoding
sourceText:
Decoding in action
Read these “pseudowords” aloud:
GLORP
SPLING
JONK
FEESH
QUISP
paragraphs: **GLORP, SPLING, JONK, FEESH and QUISP can be pronounced without being familiar words.** Their forms follow enough English spelling patterns for a reader to construct a plausible pronunciation.
Success cannot depend on retrieving a stored pronunciation for each particular item. The reader is using knowledge that generalizes across words.
The demonstration establishes generalization. By itself, it does not decide whether that knowledge consists of categorical rules or learned statistical patterns.

title: Speed of pseudoword naming
sourceText:
Pseudowords (here called “nonwords”) 
can be read nearly as quickly and 
accurately as real words.
(In this example, pseudoword naming 
times are between 5 and 12% slower than 
reading times for low-frequency words.)
This suggests that we “do” decoding fairly 
naturally, automatically and implicitly. 
Decoding in action
The questions we’ll consider when we discuss computational models of word reading 
have to do with how decoding should be characterized.
Specifically, we’ll discuss whether this behavior is best captured by categorical rules or 
probabilistic constraints. 
Lupker, Brown, & Colombo (1997)
paragraphs: **Pseudoword decoding is fast and largely automatic.** In the Lupker, Brown and Colombo example, naming pseudowords is only about 5–12% slower than naming low-frequency real words.

Participants read the items aloud, and naming time measures how quickly a pronunciation becomes available. The small difference shows that unfamiliarity does not make pronunciation an entirely slow, deliberate process.
Both rules and statistical generalization might produce efficient decoding. The speed result constrains a theory without selecting one architecture on its own.

title: Ambiguous pseudowords
sourceText:
Decoding with ambiguity
Read these pseudowords aloud:
VONTH
PHANGE
STREAD
SOUGH
paragraphs: **An unfamiliar spelling can support more than one plausible pronunciation.** VONTH, PHANGE, STREAD and SOUGH contain patterns whose pronunciations are not all uniquely determined in English.
A response reflects the spelling–sound patterns available from previously learned words. Different familiar patterns can favor different responses to the same novel form.

title: Generalization and competing patterns
sourceText:
Decoding with ambiguity
VONTH
PHANGE
STREAD
SOUGH
Generalization is a good way to test what kinds of 
regularities people have learned about a system.
Remember, e.g., The Wug Test…(or if you don’t remember, 
we’ll get to it next week)
It’s hard to imagine a rule set that covers our intuition that 
both /strɛd/ and /strid/ are acceptable for STREAD.
paragraphs: **STREAD can plausibly be pronounced with either /ɛ/ or /i/.** The same written sequence can resemble more than one learned spelling–sound pattern.
Testing novel items reveals what a reader has generalized, because the particular word cannot simply have been memorized.
The challenge for a categorical rule account is to explain why multiple outputs seem acceptable. A statistical account can represent differing support for alternative pronunciations.

title: Regularity and consistency
sourceText:
Decoding effects for real words: 
the “regularity effect”
We’ll examine arguments about the 
nature of decoding processes next 
time.
It’s uncontroversial that some form 
of decoding is part of normal 
reading, and that words that are 
“irregular” (or “inconsistent”) are 
harder to recognize than words 
that are regular.
This is straightforward for items like 
PINT, ACHE, CHOIR, etc.
It’s less clear-cut for 
“neighborhoods” of words like 
ROLL/POLL/TOLL/DOLL or 
COOK/TOOK/BOOK/SPOOK.
paragraphs: **The regularity effect is the difficulty of reading words whose pronunciation conflicts with common spelling–sound patterns.** PINT, ACHE and CHOIR are examples of words for which straightforward decoding can mislead.
A strict regular–irregular division is less clear when a spelling neighborhood contains several pronunciations. ROLL, POLL and TOLL support one pattern, while DOLL differs.
COOK, TOOK and BOOK likewise contrast with SPOOK. These neighborhoods motivate asking how much support a pronunciation has from similar words.

title: Sublexical and lexical information
sourceText:
So, we have a lot of evidence for the use of sublexical information in 
reading, especially in the translation from spelling to sound
People read nonwords quickly and accurately.
Words that follow typical spelling-to-sound patterns are easier to read than ones that don’t.
What about lexical processes?
paragraphs: **Sublexical information concerns units smaller than a whole word.** Rapid nonword reading and the advantage for typical spelling–sound patterns show that readers use this information.
**Lexical information** concerns knowledge of particular words. A complete account must explain how experience with a specific word contributes alongside general spelling patterns.

title: Interactive activation and ambiguous letters
sourceText: Well, there’s this again.
paragraphs: **Word knowledge can help identify an ambiguous letter.** In an interactive activation network, visual features activate letters and letters activate candidate words.
Activated word candidates send feedback to their constituent letters. A letter supported by a plausible word receives additional activation even when its local visual evidence is unclear.
Competing candidates do not remain equally active. Their activation changes as the network settles on an interpretation.

title: Feedback in the Interactive Activation Model
sourceText:
The Interactive Activation Model:
- feedback from activation for known words 
increases the activation for letters that occur in 
those words
paragraphs: **Feedback carries word-level activation back to letters.** A partially activated known word increases activation of the letters that belong to it.
This makes recognition interactive. Information does not flow only from isolated features upward to a finished word.
The mechanism helps explain why an ambiguous letter can become easier to recognize when it appears in a familiar word context.

title: Lexicality and frequency
sourceText:
Also note that we’ve already seen two lexical 
effects:
- the overall effect of lexicality
- the effect of word frequency.
Just as with picture naming, the number of 
times you’ve encountered a word in the past 
has an impact on how rapidly you can name it.
This effect is robust over a very very large 
number of observations 
(Balota et al. 2004, data from the English Lexicon Project)
paragraphs: **Lexicality and word frequency reveal effects of word-specific experience.** Real words are generally named faster than pseudowords, and frequently encountered words are named faster than less frequent words.
Lexicality compares whether the item is a word. Frequency compares how often a particular word has been encountered.
The English Lexicon Project data show that the frequency effect occurs across many observations, rather than depending on a few unusually easy examples.

title: Controlling confounds in frequency effects
sourceText:
Remember we worried about whether 
frequency effects might be confounds of 
length and other variables.
This appears not to be the case in a multiple 
regression analysis of about 3000 words, read 
by 30 young and older adults.
paragraphs: **Multiple regression tests whether frequency predicts reading time after accounting for other word properties.** Length and sound-related characteristics could otherwise be mistaken for effects of frequency.
The analysis uses about 3,000 words read by young and older adults. Frequency still contributes when other predictors are considered.
This makes a simple length-confound explanation less plausible. It does not turn an observational predictor into an experimentally isolated cause.

title: Frequency by regularity interaction
sourceText:
This is a landmark finding in psycholinguistics. 
We’ll see how it has impacted a number of other areas 
(most immediately inflectional morphology).
What does it mean?
The frequency effect is much 
larger for exception words 
than regular words. 
Behold: The Frequency by Regularity interaction.
paragraphs: **Frequency and regularity interact.** Low-frequency exception words are slowed much more than low-frequency regular words, whereas high-frequency words show a much smaller regularity difference.
Naming latency is the time needed to begin saying the word. Higher values mean slower responses.
An interaction means the effect of one factor depends on the other. The regularity cost is not a fixed amount added equally to high- and low-frequency words.

title: Dual-route interpretation of the interaction
sourceText:
One interpretation
There are two separate processes in word recognition: 
1. A sublexical process (decoding), and
2. A lexical process (knowledge of a particular word)
For high frequency (HF) words, the lexical process is so fast and efficient that there is little 
influence of the sublexical process.
The sublexical process only shows up when we read nonwords, or low frequency (LF) words.
paragraphs: **A dual-route interpretation separates lexical retrieval from sublexical decoding.** The lexical process supplies the learned pronunciation of a particular word, while decoding computes pronunciation from spelling units.
For a high-frequency word, lexical information becomes available quickly enough to reduce the influence of the decoding output.
For a low-frequency exception, the lexical response is less efficient and the regularized decoding output can interfere. Nonwords depend on decoding because they lack a stored whole-word entry.

title: Acquired phonological dyslexia
sourceText:
Neuropsychological evidence for these “dual 
routes”
Patients with acquired phonological dyslexia:
- present with reading difficulty as the result of brain injury (thus “acquired” as opposed 
to “developmental” dyslexia)
- have difficulty specifically with pseudoword naming.
Cacciopo van Vliet et al. (2003)
paragraphs: **Acquired phonological dyslexia involves disproportionate difficulty reading pseudowords after brain injury.** Familiar words can remain relatively well read even when novel forms are difficult.

Cacciopo van Vliet and colleagues compare real-word reading with several nonword tasks. The patients can often recognize and pronounce known words while struggling to generate a plausible pronunciation for an unfamiliar spelling.
The selective difficulty suggests that familiar-word success and novel-form decoding do not rely on every process to the same degree.

title: Acquired surface dyslexia
sourceText:
Neuropsychological evidence for these “dual 
routes”
Patients with “acquired surface dyslexia:”
- also present with reading 
difficulties after brain injury
- difficulties are specifically with 
irregular words.
- mispronunciations tend to be 
“regularizations.”
paragraphs: **Acquired surface dyslexia involves disproportionate difficulty reading irregular words after brain injury.** Errors often regularize the word by applying a more common spelling–sound pattern.
DEAF pronounced like “deef” and SHOE pronounced like “show” illustrate regularization. The response is related to the spelling, but it is not the target word's learned pronunciation.
Relatively good regular-word and nonword reading shows that generating pronunciation from spelling can remain useful despite difficulty with exceptions.

title: The reading double dissociation
sourceText:
Neuropsychological evidence for these “dual 
routes”
Patients with “acquired surface dyslexia:”
- also present with reading 
difficulties after brain injury
- difficulties are specifically with 
irregular words.
- mispronunciations tend to be 
“regularizations.”
- relatively spared pseudoword
reading.
Patients with acquired phonological dyslexia:
- present with reading difficulty as the 
result of brain injury (thus “acquired” as 
opposed to “developmental” dyslexia)
- have difficulty specifically with 
pseudoword naming.
- relatively spared exception word reading
This is a classic double dissociation.
paragraphs: **A double dissociation compares opposite relative impairments.** Phonological dyslexia particularly affects pseudowords, while surface dyslexia particularly affects exception words.

The first pattern shows that unfamiliar decoding can be difficult despite relatively preserved familiar-word reading. The second shows that exception reading can be difficult despite relatively preserved pseudoword reading.
Together, the patterns are harder to explain by saying that one task is simply harder for everyone.

title: Why double dissociations matter
sourceText: Why are double dissociations so powerful?
paragraphs: **A double dissociation challenges a single fixed difficulty ranking.** If task A were merely harder than task B, damage might consistently hurt A more, but it would not readily explain another patient showing the reverse pattern.
The reversal suggests that the tasks depend differently on underlying processes. For reading, pseudowords and exception words place different demands on the system.
The evidence still requires a theory of what those underlying processes are. It does not uniquely identify a particular set of boxes in a model.

title: Locating deficits in a dual-route model
sourceText:
Why are double dissociations so powerful?
They provide evidence that processes underlying 
pseudoword and irregular word reading (for example) 
are separable.
In this model, we can imagine:
- phonological dyslexia results from specific
damage to the grapheme-phoneme conversion 
module
- surface dyslexia results from damage to input 
or output “logogens”, or the connections between 
them
paragraphs: **A dual-route model attributes phonological dyslexia to damage in grapheme–phoneme conversion and surface dyslexia to damage in lexical processing.** These proposed locations connect the task dissociation to specific mechanisms.
Damage to conversion particularly affects nonwords because there is no familiar whole-word pronunciation to retrieve.
Damage to input or output word representations, called logogens in this account, or their connections makes exceptions vulnerable because general decoding supplies the wrong pronunciation.

title: Complications for a strict two-route account
sourceText:
Patterson (1981, British Journal of Psychology)
Early inklings that it is not so simple…
paragraphs: **Patterson's discussion shows why reading errors can complicate a clean lexical–nonlexical division.** Errors attributed to a purely nonlexical route can still show lexical influences.
The example “incense” read as “increase” is a real-word response. A simple letter–sound mistake could instead produce a nonword, so the actual response raises a question about whole-word influence.

Possible responses are to allow a more complicated combination of routes or to revise the supposedly nonlexical process itself. The observation motivates refinement rather than settling the issue alone.

title: Reading 2 · Computational models
sourceText:
Reading 2: Computational 
models

title: Why propose two reading routes?
sourceText:
Dual route models of visual word recognition 
This general form of model is motivated by the 
phenomena we reviewed in the last lecture:
- pseudoword reading is fast and automatic
- word reading is faster
- reading is fastest for high-frequency words
- accuracy and response time are also 
impacted by “regularity”
- frequency and regularity interact
- pseudoword reading and irregular word 
reading are dissociable in acquired dyslexia
Thus, the model hypothesize 
- a sublexical route for grapheme-to-
phoneme conversion (decoding)
- a lexical route for recognizing real words
paragraphs: **Dual-route models distinguish a lexical route from a sublexical route.** Lexical processing uses knowledge of particular words, while grapheme–phoneme conversion generates pronunciation from spelling units.
A model must explain fast pseudoword reading, faster familiar-word reading, frequency effects, regularity effects and their interaction.
It must also explain why pseudoword and exception-word reading can be differently impaired after brain injury. These observations motivate the architecture but do not uniquely prove it.

title: The Dual Route Cascaded model
sourceText:
(image credit: http://www.maccs.mq.edu.au/~ssaunder/DRC/)
Coltheart et al. (2001, Psych Review)
This is the “DRC -- Dual Route 
Cascaded” model. 
Some key points:
The portion circled in red is 
just the Interactive Activation 
model.
There is no implementation 
of semantics, since both the 
orthographic and phonological 
lexicons are independent of 
semantics.
The Grapheme-Phoneme 
Rule System has completely 
different processing assumptions 
from the interactive portion of the 
model.
paragraphs: **The Dual Route Cascaded model, or DRC, combines interactive lexical processing with a separate grapheme–phoneme rule system.** The two routes can contribute activation toward a spoken response.
The lexical portion includes orthographic and phonological lexicons, representing written and spoken word forms. These representations are distinguished from meanings.
The implementation described here does not implement semantics. The GPC rule system also has processing assumptions different from those of the interactive lexical network.

title: How GPC processing works
sourceText:
Some important features of the 
Grapheme-Phoneme Rule System:
Its rules are activated serially, 
letter by letter. 
It is not affected by frequency 
of occurrence in any way.
It has no feedback. 
It does not interact with the 
lexical route, except in the 
phoneme response buffer, where 
it is connected to the same output 
units (and therefore can compete 
to activate different patterns).
(image credit: http://www.maccs.mq.edu.au/~ssaunder/DRC/)
Coltheart et al. (2001, Psych Review)
paragraphs: **The DRC's grapheme–phoneme conversion rules operate serially, letter by letter.** Their operation is not adjusted by word frequency and receives no lexical feedback.
The GPC and lexical routes do not interact throughout their internal computations. They converge in the phoneme response buffer.
If the routes favor different phonemes, they can compete at that shared output. An exception word can therefore receive a correct lexical pronunciation and an incompatible regularized pronunciation.

title: Rules and rules for applying rules
sourceText:
What are the GPC rules like?
<...>
(you also need some meta-rules for 
when to apply rules at different levels of 
analysis, e.g., larger-unit rules 
supersede smaller-unit rules)
paragraphs: **GPC rules map written units onto phonemes.** Some rules concern individual letters, while others concern several letters or a particular letter context.
A model also needs a way to decide which applicable rule takes priority. A larger-unit rule can supersede rules for its individual letters.
Context-sensitive rules restrict a pronunciation to specified surrounding letters or positions. This makes the procedure more than a simple lookup of one sound per letter.

title: Categorical rules and statistical support
sourceText:
Actually, the rules aren’t totally independent of statistics.
They’re often based on the most frequent pronunciation for a letter or 
combination of letters.
But they are fixed and categorical. So, even though the rule for -OUGH has 
weaker statistical support than the rule for -EIGH, they are both rules and 
behave the same way during processing.

paragraphs: **A categorical rule does not express the strength of the evidence behind it.** The DRC can choose a mapping because it is frequent, yet treat that mapping as a fixed rule during processing.
The possible pronunciations of OUGH have more divided statistical support than those of EIGH. A rule can still operate categorically for both spellings.

A probabilistic account instead allows alternatives to receive different strengths of support. The distinction concerns processing, not whether the model designer ever consulted frequency information.

title: Why imperfect rules were defended
sourceText:
…by which I mean that they seem to miss a lot of cases.
This was seen as a feature, though, not a bug.
We could certainly come up with better rules if we took statistics into account more flexibly. 
(In fact the DRC’s rules went through several revisions to improve its nonword reading.)
But the argument from the DRC is that people don’t use such finely-tuned rules for the GPC 
route. 
If they did, you wouldn’t see the pattern of regularization errors that you see in surface 
dyslexia, or the slow-down in performance that you see for low-frequency exception words. 
These rules are kind of silly
paragraphs: **The DRC's simple rules are intended to explain systematic human errors as well as correct reading.** More finely tuned rules might pronounce more exceptions correctly but remove behavior the model is meant to explain.
A regularizing route helps account for errors in surface dyslexia and for slow naming of low-frequency exception words.
The theory therefore claims that people's sublexical computation is constrained, rather than assuming that the best possible spelling algorithm is the correct cognitive model.

title: Informational encapsulation
sourceText:
Remember when we talked about models of syntax?
We saw that parsing strategies like “late closure” and 
“minimal attachment” were motivated by 
consideration of syntactic complexity only.
The idea was to explain syntactic processing as 
informationally encapsulated from world knowledge, 
lexical co-occurrence statistics, etc.
The dual-route models are designed to be similarly 
modular. 
The GPC chugs along and produces correct 
pronunciations for many words, incorrect responses 
to some “exceptions” to its rules. Occasionally, we can 
observe its operation when:
-people produce “regularization” errors
- we force people to name pseudowords
These rules are kind of silly
paragraphs: **Informational encapsulation means that a process does not freely use every source of relevant knowledge.** In the dual-route account, GPC conversion proceeds without consulting whole-word meaning or lexical feedback.
This resembles a modular parsing proposal in which an early syntactic process follows structural principles without immediately using world knowledge.
Pseudoword naming exposes the conversion procedure because a familiar lexical entry is unavailable. Regularization errors expose it when conversion favors the wrong pronunciation.

title: Breadth of DRC simulations
sourceText:
The DRC can simulate a lot of phenomena in visual 
word recognition. 
Coltheart et al., 2001, Psych Review
paragraphs: **The DRC is evaluated against many reading phenomena.** These include frequency, lexicality, regularity, interactions, lexical decision and patterns in acquired dyslexia.
Accounting for several effects with one architecture is stronger than fitting a single result. It also requires examining which assumptions stay fixed and which are changed between tasks.
The model's research strategy places strong weight on human behavioral evidence as a constraint on architecture.

title: Modeling lexical decision
sourceText:
This sometimes means going to extremes to make contact with data
Reduce letter-word inhibition. 
(This change makes the task harder, but 
without it, the results make no sense.) 
If any single word has an activity above a 
threshold of 0.69, answer “yes.”
If the activity over the orthographic 
input lexicon exceeds threshold S, 
answer “yes.”
(where S = 10 from 0-20 cycles, and is 
then reduced to 1.98 if activity in the 
orthographic lexicon exceeds 0.2 at 20 
cycles).
If neither of these criteria is met by D 
cycles, answer “no.”
(where D = 42 unless activity in the 
lexicon exceeds 0.112 after 20 cycles, in 
which case it is set to 48. Note that this 
nearly twice as fast as the model 
normally reads aloud).
How the lexical decision task is 
modeled in the DRC…
paragraphs: **Lexical decision requires deciding whether a written item is a word.** The DRC simulation adds decision criteria to the activation produced by its recognition system.
A “yes” response can depend on a strongly activated single word or on total activity across the orthographic lexicon. A “no” response occurs if the criteria are not met by a deadline.
The implementation also changes inhibition and uses time-dependent thresholds. These choices help obtain a fit, but they add assumptions beyond the basic two-route diagram.

title: Modularity in the DRC
sourceText:
Key feature of the DRC: Modularity
The GPC route and lexical route:
- each have their own processing assumptions
- are informationally encapsulated from one another
- are domain-specific, i.e., the GPC rules can only take letters as 
inputs and pass phoneme activations to the phoneme system
paragraphs: **The DRC routes are modular in several related senses.** They use different processing assumptions, restrict information exchange and accept particular kinds of input.
The GPC system takes letters as input and sends phoneme activation toward the response system. This is **domain specificity** in the account.
The absence of lexical feedback into the GPC system is **informational encapsulation**. Having two pathways alone would not establish those stronger restrictions.

title: An emergentist reading model
sourceText:
An emergentist approach: PDP models of visual word 
recognition
Seidenberg & McClelland (1989)
Conceived of reading skill as emerging from mappings 
among spelling, pronunciation, and meaning.
Modeled the learning of these mappings by training a 
simple associative network. 
Studied mappings from orthography to phonology (O 
P) in a single “route.”
paragraphs: **PDP models treat reading as learned mappings among orthography, phonology and semantics.** Orthography is spelling, phonology is sound structure, and semantics is meaning.
Seidenberg and McClelland trained an associative network to map spelling onto pronunciation. The modeled spelling-to-sound pathway used one learned mapping for different kinds of words.
Reading skill emerges from learning rather than being specified entirely as a hand-built list of rules and lexical entries.

title: Distributed knowledge and general learning
sourceText:
PDP models of visual word recognition
Seidenberg & McClelland (1989)
Different assumptions from dual-route models:
- “rules” are just generalizations from lots of 
words, not a separate process
- the “lexicon” is also distributed. Some 
whole-word information is stored in O P 
mappings, some in  other parts of the system.
Different research strategy from dual-route 
models:
Explain reading in terms of domain-general 
learning mechanisms, rather than reverse-
engineer the system from adult/neuropsych data.
paragraphs: **In a PDP account, rules are generalizations learned across words.** Whole-word knowledge is distributed across learned mappings instead of being stored only in a distinct lexical route.
The same learning mechanism can capture both patterns shared by many words and information specific to a familiar word.
The research strategy asks whether domain-general learning can explain reading. This contrasts with choosing separate adult processing components primarily from neuropsychological dissociations.

title: Learning the frequency–regularity interaction
sourceText:
Frequency by regularity interaction
The model captured the interaction between 
frequency and regularity without assuming 
that these effects resulted from different 
processes.
How?
- “regular” words are consistent with 
statistical patterns from many other words.
- “exception” words are inconsistent with 
these statistics.
- frequency also impacts how well words 
are learned. So, highly frequent words are 
less effected by inconsistency with other 
words.
paragraphs: **A learned network can produce a frequency-by-regularity interaction without separate frequency and rule mechanisms.** Regular words receive support from patterns shared across many words.
An exception conflicts with those patterns, so learning its particular mapping is especially important. Frequent exposure strengthens that word-specific mapping.
A low-frequency exception has both weak item-specific learning and poor support from the dominant pattern. This combination creates a larger disadvantage than either factor alone.

title: Consistency rather than a single rule boundary
sourceText:
Redefining “regularity”
Regular Consistent: Many friends and no 
enemies [LATE, DUST]
Regular Inconsistent: Many friends but at 
least one enemy [GAVE (cf.HAVE), MINT 
(cf.PINT)]
Ambiguous: About equal numbers of 
friends and enemies [DOWN, KNOWN; 
POUR, SOUR] 
Exception: Few if any friends and many 
enemies [HAVE (cf. GAVE), PINT (cf. 
MINT)]
paragraphs: **Consistency describes how many similar spellings support a pronunciation.** “Friends” have the relevant spelling pattern and a compatible pronunciation, while “enemies” support a competing pronunciation.
LATE and DUST illustrate consistent patterns. GAVE and MINT have many friends but also enemies such as HAVE and PINT.
DOWN versus KNOWN and POUR versus SOUR illustrate ambiguity. An exception such as PINT has relatively little support compared with its competing neighborhood.

title: Using learned weights for nonwords
sourceText:
Reading words and nonwords in the same 
“route”
In principle: 
- nonwords named via the same set of weights used 
for words.
- generalization takes advantage of the same statistical 
patterns that give rise to regularity effects.
paragraphs: **A PDP model can pronounce nonwords using the weights learned from real words.** A new spelling activates patterns that overlap with familiar spellings, allowing the network to generalize.
No stored entry for the particular nonword is required. The same learned correspondences that support consistent words can support a new combination.
This is a proposed mechanism for decoding without a separate GPC rule module.

title: Theory versus implementation
sourceText:
In practice, though, not so great…
Nonword accuracy was not very 
good.
Why?
This is a classic case of ambiguity in 
model evaluation.
Was the theoretical claim -- that 
nonwords and exceptions could 
be read by the same, associative 
mechanism – wrong?
Or, was the problem something 
specific to the way the model was 
made?
paragraphs: **Poor nonword performance can challenge either a theoretical proposal or a particular implementation.** The early model's nonword accuracy was weaker than desired.
One possibility is that a single associative mechanism cannot explain the task. Another is that the chosen representations fail to capture the similarities needed for generalization.
Improving the implementation while retaining the theoretical mechanism helps distinguish these possibilities.

title: Phonological representation matters
sourceText:
Nonword reading related to phonological representations
Many studies demonstrate a 
relationship between “decoding” 
(i.e., nonword reading) and 
phonological processing.
The phonological representations 
used in Seidenberg & McClelland 
were sort of weird:  Wickelfeatures.
Indeed, a model by Plaut et al. (1996, 
Psych Review) improved the 
phonological representations, and 
produced better performance on 
nonwords.
paragraphs: **Generalization depends on how sound similarity is represented.** The early Seidenberg–McClelland model used Wickelfeatures, whose representation of phonology was problematic for nonword reading.
Plaut and colleagues improved the phonological representations and obtained better nonword performance. This supports a representational explanation for at least part of the earlier failure.
Behavioral relations between phonological processing and decoding also make phonology a relevant target for explanation.

title: Why degraded phonology hurts generalization
sourceText:
How are phonological representations and 
nonword generalization related?
Generalization depends on similarity. (In fact this principle is 
inherited from behaviorism.)
Poor phonological representations (like Wickelfeatures) fail to 
adequately capture the similarity space of words in the language.
Word-specific information is more robust to poor representations, 
because it doesn’t depend entirely on generalization.
paragraphs: **A network generalizes through similarity.** If its phonological representation poorly captures similarities among words, the learned mapping cannot transfer as effectively to new forms.
A familiar word can retain support from its own training history. A nonword lacks that item-specific experience and depends more heavily on generalization.
This produces a reason for unfamiliar forms to be especially vulnerable to poor representations without requiring a dedicated nonword mechanism.

title: Harm and Seidenberg's noise manipulation
sourceText:
How are phonological representations and 
nonword generalization related?
Harm & Seidenberg (1999) investigated 
this more systematically, by 
manipulating the amount of “noise” in 
the phonological representations.
They were able to replicate a number of 
key findings in the literature on 
developmental dyslexia:
- relationship between degree of 
phonological deficit and phonological 
dyslexia
- relative sparing of word recognition
paragraphs: **Harm and Seidenberg manipulated noise in phonological representations.** Increasing noise makes the sound representations less reliable while keeping the model's general learning framework.
The manipulation produced poorer nonword decoding and relative sparing of word recognition. It also linked the severity of the phonological deficit to the degree of decoding difficulty.
The model therefore connects a reading pattern to the quality of a more general phonological system.

title: Semantics and surface dyslexia
sourceText:
What about all of those double-dissociations?
We’ve already seen how nonword
reading can be specifically impaired, 
despite the model’s lack of a specific 
“nonword reading mechanism.”
Plaut et al. (1996) explored the other 
end of this dissociation: surface 
dyslexia. 
To do this, they implemented a 
simplified semantic system, and 
demonstrated that lesions to 
semantics resulted in a specific 
impairment on “exception” words.
paragraphs: **Damaging semantic support in a triangle model can impair exception-word reading especially strongly.** Plaut and colleagues added a simplified semantic contribution and examined what happened when it was lesioned.
An exception has weak support from typical spelling–sound regularities. Meaning-related support can help produce its learned pronunciation.
Reducing that support creates a surface-dyslexia-like pattern without defining a separate exception-word list as the sole explanation.

title: Why the triangle is not just DRC renamed
sourceText:
Why is this not just the dual route model now?
Semantic representations are directly involved, as opposed 
to a theoretical commitment to a lexicon independent 
of semantics.
[A later model (Harm & Seidenberg, 2004) would 
implement featural semantics, and simulate the 
mapping of spelling to meaning.]
The OP and SP mappings have the same processing 
assumptions and learning algorithm. Both are 
probabilistic. 
A key point of these simulations is that these pathways interact over the course of 
learning. So, the OP pathway develops differently in the context of an OSP 
pathway than it would otherwise.
This interactivity and gradedness permits the models to capture the fact that double 
dissociations are never entirely “clean.”
- Phonological dyslexics are not perfect on exception words. 
- Surface dyslexics are not perfect on nonwords.
paragraphs: **The triangle model's pathways share graded learning assumptions and interact during learning.** Semantic representations are directly involved rather than replaced by a lexicon defined as independent of meaning.
Spelling-to-sound learning develops in the presence of meaning-related support. The contribution of one pathway therefore affects what another pathway learns.
This allows graded impairments. Phonological dyslexics can make some exception errors, and surface dyslexics can make some nonword errors.

title: Semantics and exception reading in patients
sourceText:
Model predicts a strong association between 
semantic abilities and exception word reading 
(Woollams et al., 2007)
paragraphs: **Woollams and colleagues tested the predicted association between semantic ability and exception-word reading.** Lower semantic scores were associated with poorer low-frequency exception reading in patients with semantic dementia.
The model and patient panels show comparable overall relationships, although individual patients vary. This supports an association between meaning and exceptional pronunciation.
The finding is informative because it links a reading weakness to a broader semantic measure rather than describing only a reading-task dissociation.

title: Interpreting apparent exceptions
sourceText:
…this means the model misses a few data 
points
What should we make of 
this?
Patients to the left of the 
vertical line, and above the 
horizontal line are statistical 
outliers.
Woollams et al. would argue 
that these observations 
should be treated the way 
we normally treat outliers 
when evaluating the fit of a 
model to data…
paragraphs: **Some patients have relatively good exception reading despite low semantic scores.** These cases challenge a perfect one-to-one relationship, but an account of graded association does not predict zero variability.
Woollams and colleagues interpret such observations in relation to the full distribution rather than treating each outlier as an automatic refutation.
The scientific issue is whether the unusual cases show a stable separate pattern or arise within a noisy overall association.

title: Following semantic dementia over time
sourceText:
Further, because they were studying 
patients with a progressive
condition (semantic dementia) they 
could observe how exception word 
reading changed as semantic 
abilities declined.
In most cases, when a patient’s 
semantic abilities declined over 
time, her reading ability also 
declined.
Note also the regression to the 
mean with multiple observations. If 
the dissociation between semantics 
and exception word reading were 
due to idiosyncratic outliers, it 
would show just this pattern.
paragraphs: **Longitudinal observations track whether semantic and reading abilities change together within a patient.** Because semantic dementia progresses, repeated testing can reveal a trajectory rather than a single unusual score.
In most cases, declining semantic ability accompanies declining exception-word reading. Some initially unusual observations move closer to the broader relation on retesting.
This strengthens the association while leaving room for variability between individuals.

title: Fitting the same patients with DRC
sourceText:
DRC simulation of the same data
Coltheart et al. (2009, Psych Review) 
simulated surface dyslexia by 
generating a population of 40,000 
model “patients” varying on two 
parameters:
- integrity of lexical route
- integrity of GPC rules
For each patient in the Woollams et al. 
data, they then selected the run of the 
model that best fit that patient’s data.
In this way, they produce an excellent 
fit to the data.
paragraphs: **Coltheart and colleagues generated 40,000 model patients with different lexical-route and GPC impairment levels.** For each real patient, they selected the model run that best matched the observed data.
This produced an excellent fit to the patient scores. The selection procedure is part of how that fit was achieved.
The fit should be distinguished from predicting each patient's pattern before choosing among many possible parameter combinations.

title: Fit and explanatory constraint
sourceText:
Why would anyone argue that a better fit to the data 
is actually a bad thing in this case?
paragraphs: **A better fit can be less informative if it relies on much greater flexibility.** Selecting the best match from many parameter combinations can reproduce a dataset without strongly constraining the underlying explanation.
The question is not whether close agreement is bad in itself. It is whether the account predicts the relation with principled assumptions or accommodates each case after seeing the outcome.
Comparing theories therefore requires attention to both fit and how much freedom produced it.

title: Shared targets for competing models
sourceText:
Comparison of dual-route and “triangle” models.
Both models cover a range of data about reading, including some basic facts:
- decoding is fast and automatic (e.g., pseudoword reading)
- words that diverge from typical spelling-to-sound mappings are harder to read
- this “regularity” or “consistency” effect interacts with word frequency
- pseudoword reading and “exception” or “inconsistent” word reading are dissociable 
in neuropsych patients
paragraphs: **Dual-route and triangle models address many of the same findings.** Both must explain rapid nonword decoding, exception difficulty, the frequency–regularity interaction and acquired reading dissociations.
Agreement on the phenomena does not mean agreement on mechanisms. One account emphasizes specialized routes, while the other emphasizes learning across interacting representational systems.

title: Comparing explanations across models
sourceText:
Comparison of dual-route and “triangle” models.
Triangle
Dual-Route
Phenomenon
Statistical regularities 
learned over many words
Dedicated “grapheme-
phoneme conversion” (GPC) 
rule system
Pseudoword reading and 
regularity effects
More exposure to a word = 
better learning for that 
word
Distinct lexicons for input 
and output, separate from 
GPC rules
Frequency effects
Deficit/damage in 
phonological processing, 
generally
Deficit/damage in the GPC 
route
Phonological dyslexia
Deficit/damage in semantic 
processes, generally
Deficit/damage in the lexical 
route
Surface dyslexia
paragraphs: **DRC attributes nonword decoding and regularity effects to GPC rules, while the triangle account attributes them to statistical learning.** Word-specific exposure strengthens learned mappings in the triangle account and affects lexical processing in DRC.
For phonological dyslexia, DRC emphasizes GPC damage and the triangle account emphasizes broader phonological impairment.
For surface dyslexia, DRC emphasizes lexical-route damage and the triangle account emphasizes semantic impairment.

title: Dissociations and associations
sourceText:
Comparison of dual-route and “triangle” models.
Triangle
Dual-Route
Phenomenon
Deficit/damage in 
phonological processing, 
generally
Deficit/damage in the GPC 
route
Phonological dyslexia
Deficit/damage in semantic 
processes, generally
Deficit/damage in the lexical 
route
Surface dyslexia
This is a key contrast: 
Dual route models (generally) are motivated by double-dissociations: 
Pseudowords and exception words can be impaired independently, so they should be 
modeled as independent processes.
Models informed by statistical learning instead reveal associations: Phonology is 
important for learning/using OP generalizations; semantics is important for words 
where OP generalization is ambiguous.
paragraphs: **A major contrast is whether the explanation begins with separate reading routes or broader language associations.** Dual-route models use different task impairments to motivate independent processes.
The statistical-learning account links phonology to spelling–sound generalization and semantics to words whose pronunciation is poorly supported by that generalization.
Both dissociations and associations matter. A theory should explain selective weaknesses and the related abilities that vary with them.

title: Reading assignment
sourceText:
For next time:
Read Joanisse (2004) “Specific Language Impairments in Children”
http://publish.uwo.ca/~marcj/joanisse-cdps-2004.pdf

title: Inflectional morphology and language impairment
sourceText: More modeling: The case of inflectional morphology and specific language impairment

title: Generative morphology
sourceText:
Quick review
Morphology is “generative”

For example, at some point there was no noun “generative,” just the verb “to generate.” But English has a process for turning verbs into nouns. That’s derivational morphology.

Today we’re going to focus on inflectional morphology. In English this pretty much means the plural and the past tense.
paragraphs: **Morphology is generative because speakers can form words they have not memorized individually.** Derivational morphology creates a new lexical form, while inflection marks grammatical information such as plural or past tense.
The central question is how a speaker extends a familiar pattern to a new item. English plural and past-tense formation provide tractable examples.
Generalization can also produce playful or incorrect forms. This shows productive use of patterns, rather than a vocabulary containing only previously heard responses.

title: The wug test
sourceText:
Classic study by Jean Berko Gleason (1958).

Demonstrates how readily people generalize the past tense to new words.

Children do this too (thus the cute drawings).
The “wug” test
paragraphs: **Berko Gleason's wug test measures morphological generalization to a novel word.** A child learns a new label and then supplies an inflected form that has not been provided.
The pictured task introduces one WUG and then asks about two. Producing WUGS applies plural knowledge to a new noun.
The same logic can test past tense using novel verbs. Success shows productive knowledge, but does not by itself distinguish symbolic rules from statistical generalization.

title: Regular and irregular past tense
sourceText:
The English past tense has “regular” and “irregular” forms.
Regulars
show-showed, bake-baked, wade-waded
blick-blicked, trog-trogged, wumble-wumbled 

Irregulars
go-went, take-took, eat-ate, sleep-slept

This should remind you right away of the last few lectures…
paragraphs: **Regular past tense follows the productive -ed pattern.** SHOW becomes SHOWED, BAKE becomes BAKED, and a novel verb such as BLICK can become BLICKED.
Irregular pairs such as GO–WENT, TAKE–TOOK and EAT–ATE do not follow that default form. Some irregulars share smaller patterns with other verbs.
A theory must explain both familiar exceptions and productive extension to novel verbs.

title: Words and Rules
sourceText:
Words and Rules
Pinker & colleagues
‘words and rules’ are separate processes, representational formats, etc.

Regulars: 
symbolic rules (e.g., “add –ed”)

Irregulars: 
lexicalized within “associative network”
paragraphs: **The Words and Rules account gives regular and irregular inflection different mechanisms.** A symbolic rule generates a regular past tense, while irregular forms are stored in an associative lexical system.
The regular process can apply to a new verb because it does not require an entry for that particular past tense.

The irregular system stores word-specific information and can be influenced by frequency and similarity. A successful explanation also needs to prevent an available irregular form from being replaced by a regularization.

title: A dual-process past-tense architecture
sourceText:
A “dual route” model for the past tense
Pinker & Ullman (2002, TICS)
How is this similar to the dual-route model we were just considering for reading?


How is it different?
paragraphs: **The lexicon and grammar offer different ways to produce a past tense.** Lexical retrieval supplies an irregular form such as HELD, while grammatical combination can produce WALK plus -ed.
Pinker and Ullman's diagram associates lexical lookup with declarative memory and grammatical combination with procedural processing.

Like dual-route reading, the account separates word-specific knowledge from a productive operation. Unlike reading aloud, its task is to transform a stem according to a grammatical feature, rather than convert spelling into sound.

title: Why separate rules from exceptions?
sourceText:
Similar architecture, different origins
Remember the dual route model was developed based on neuropsychological double-dissociations.

Pinker et al. are motivated by other concerns.

Generative linguistics of the time was mostly about categorical, symbolic, rule-based grammars.

These rules often have exceptions.
paragraphs: **The Words and Rules proposal was motivated partly by a theory of grammar.** A categorical symbolic grammar describes productive patterns, but language also contains exceptions.

Reading dual-route theories were strongly motivated by neuropsychological dissociations. The morphology proposal also reflects a commitment to keeping the grammatical rule system distinct from exceptional lexical information.

title: Properties of the exception system
sourceText:
Similar architecture, different origins
Rather than make the grammar inelegant by adding machinery to handle the exceptions, linguists would often just leave the exceptions out of the grammar.

So dual-process model proposes a way to “handle” the exceptions while keeping the grammar elegant, symbolic, categorical, etc.

This second process had all the properties the rule route did not. It was:
	  - word-specific (lexical)
		- sensitive to frequency of occurrence
	  - sensitive to phonological similarity (keep-kept, weep-wept, leap-leapt, etc.)
paragraphs: **An associative lexicon handles information that does not fit a categorical rule.** Its representations are word-specific and sensitive to frequency and phonological similarity.
KEEP–KEPT, WEEP–WEPT and LEAP–LEAPT illustrate similarity among irregular forms. An exception can belong to a small family rather than being wholly unrelated to other words.
Assigning these properties to lexical memory lets the rule system remain categorical and general.

title: An associative alternative
sourceText:
An alternative approach: It’s all associative learning!
Rumelhart & McClelland (1987) available, along with lots of these other papers, here: http://psych.stanford.edu/~jlm/papers/
paragraphs: **Rumelhart and McClelland modeled past tense as a learned association between present and past sound patterns.** A single trainable network learns across verbs instead of applying a separately specified -ed rule.
The model encodes a root's phonology, transforms that representation through modifiable connections, and decodes an output pattern.
Regularity is a pattern learned from many examples. Irregular forms are also learned within the same system.

title: U-shaped learning
sourceText:
Target phenomena of Rumelhart & McClelland
Because this was one of the first learning models to address a language process, the focus was on capturing developmental phenomena.

Specifically: “U-shaped” learning:

	- some frequent irregular verbs are learned quite early, e.g., run-ran

	- then, spontaneously, children begin producing “regularizations:” runned.

	- eventually, they start producing correct forms again.

Learning is “U-shaped” because children often get worse before they get better, so performance goes down before it goes back up.
paragraphs: **U-shaped learning describes an initial success, a decline, and later recovery.** A child may correctly say RAN, later produce RUNNED, and eventually return to RAN.
The middle error is a **regularization**, because the child applies the common past-tense pattern to an irregular verb.
The decline does not necessarily mean that the child has stopped learning. A changing system can generalize more broadly while temporarily disrupting an earlier correct response.

title: Words and Rules interpretation of development
sourceText:
Why is U-shaped learning important to the “words and rules” approach? 
It’s understood in terms of distinct stages/processes:

	- early correct forms are just imitations, don’t depend on the same mechanisms as adult processing.

	- when the rule is initially learned, it is applied to all cases. We can think of the rule as the “best hypothesis” for all items generally.

	- over time, exceptions are learned associatively, one-by-one and incorporated into lexical knowledge. Further, the “blocking process” develops.
paragraphs: **The Words and Rules account explains U-shaped learning through changes in the use of rules and lexical exceptions.** Early correct forms can be imitated before a productive rule is available.
When the rule is learned, it can be applied too broadly, yielding RUNNED. Later, learned irregulars and the blocking process prevent that regularization.
This account treats the developmental stages as involving distinguishable processes rather than only gradual changes in one mapping.

title: U-shaped learning in an associative model
sourceText:
“U-shaped learning” in Rumelhart & McClellands’s model.

 - training set is based on data about input to children, which changes over time.

 Early on, irregular verbs predominate – in fact the highest-frequency verbs tend to have irregular past-tense forms: GIVE, TAKE, HAVE, GO, etc.

 As the vocabulary expands to include more regular forms, the model reorganizes to capture those regularities.

- this interferes with some of the early-learned forms.
paragraphs: **Changing the training vocabulary can produce U-shaped learning in one network.** Early training emphasizes frequent irregular verbs, allowing those particular mappings to be learned.
As more regular verbs enter training, their common pattern changes the network's responses. That generalization can interfere with previously learned irregulars.
With further learning, the network can recover the irregular responses while retaining broad regularity. No new symbolic rule component is inserted at the point of decline.

title: Testing model generalization
sourceText:
Generalization testing:

The model was trained on a small number of verbs, so they could do a “wug” test with real words…
paragraphs: **Testing untrained verbs asks whether the network learned transferable structure.** A real English verb can be novel to a model if it was excluded from that model's training set.
The test therefore uses the logic of a wug task even when the items are real words to humans.
The model can generate many appropriate past-tense features, but feature-level success must be distinguished from producing an entirely correct word.

title: Unusual model outputs
sourceText: But…
paragraphs: **Some model outputs contain changes that are unlike ordinary human regularizations.** Examples include MADE(D)-like changes to MATE and the unusual outputs MEMBLED for MAIL and TOUREDER for TOUR.
The model authors acknowledge that people are unlikely to make some of these errors. They suggest that additional output constraints could reduce bizarre responses.
This separates capturing an overall learning pattern from matching the detailed form of human errors.

title: The blending criticism
sourceText: Prince & Pinker (1988, BBS)
paragraphs: **Prince and Pinker argued that feature representations can blend distinct alternatives.** A model may activate features belonging to several possible past-tense forms without keeping those candidates separate.
For SING, partial support for different sound patterns can overlap. Decoding the combined activation can produce a hybrid rather than selecting a coherent word.
The criticism targets the representation and its treatment of competing outputs, not merely the presence of learning.

title: Phonology and semantics in inflection
sourceText:
A new(er) model: Joanisse & Seidenberg (1999)
Theoretical premise:

	- “rule-like” generalization is supported by phonological representations

 	- “irregular” forms require greater support from semantics
paragraphs: **Joanisse and Seidenberg propose that phonology supports rule-like generalization while semantics especially supports irregular forms.** The same system links speech input, meaning and speech output.
Reliable sound representations support extension from familiar present–past pairs to new forms. Irregular mappings receive additional support from the particular word's semantic representation.
The hypothesis concerns different degrees of dependence on shared systems, rather than a separate symbolic rule route for every regular response.

title: Targeting a neuropsychological dissociation
sourceText:
A new(er) model: Joanisse & Seidenberg (1999)
Target phenomenon:

	- dissociation between irregular and nonword past tense in neuropsychological data.
paragraphs: **The model aims to explain the dissociation between irregular and nonword past-tense performance.** These tasks differ in how much they depend on learned word-specific information and phonological generalization.
A nonword has no familiar item-specific semantic history to support its inflection. A known irregular can require semantic support because its output is not well predicted by the dominant pattern.
Manipulating phonological or semantic integrity tests whether these different dependencies can produce opposite impairment profiles.

title: Broca's aphasia and novel past tense
sourceText:
Neuropsychological data
Broca’s Aphasia
Injury to left anterior brain regions

Poor speech production

Problems with regular morphology, esp. nonwords
wug  wugged, 
blick   blicked
paragraphs: **The patient pattern associated here with Broca's aphasia includes especially poor nonword past-tense production.** These patients have left anterior injury and difficulty producing speech.
Regular forms are also vulnerable, while irregular forms are relatively better in the displayed comparison. A novel BLICK must be transformed without relying on a familiar stored past tense.
This motivates investigating phonological contributions to the apparent morphological deficit.

title: Phonological damage in the model
sourceText:
Phonological Impairment in the Model
Reduced ability to compute past tense forms

Nonwords worse than regulars and irregulars

Regulars numerically worse than irregulars
paragraphs: **Phonological impairment reduces past-tense performance most strongly for nonwords in the model.** Regulars are numerically worse than irregulars, but the largest difference concerns novel forms.
The model manipulation weakens sound-based computation. Familiar words retain support unavailable to an untrained nonword.
The similarity to the patient pattern shows how a selective-looking morphological deficit can arise from a broader phonological impairment.

title: Patients with irregular-form difficulties
sourceText:
Neuropsychological data: Problems with irregulars
Wernicke’s and Alzheimer’s patients
Anomic patients with injury to inferior/middle temporal brain regions

Poor on irregulars (middle bar)
paragraphs: **Other patient groups show a larger problem with irregular past-tense forms.** The material discusses Wernicke's and Alzheimer's patients and anomic patients with inferior or middle temporal injury.
Their irregular performance is lower than their regular and nonword performance in the displayed comparison.
This creates the other side of the dissociation and motivates examining the information that especially supports known irregular forms.

title: Semantic damage in the model
sourceText:
Effects of Semantic Impairment
Irregulars worse than regulars and nonwords

Nonwords a bit worse than regulars
paragraphs: **Semantic impairment particularly disrupts irregular past-tense forms.** When the model loses meaning-related support, irregular accuracy falls below regular and nonword accuracy.
Typical phonological patterns still support many regular and novel forms. Nonwords can nevertheless be somewhat worse than regular words because they lack item-specific training.
This shows how unequal dependence on semantics can produce the reverse of the phonological-damage profile.

title: Testing the double-dissociation interpretation
sourceText:
Broca’s patients:
Differences between regulars and irregulars are reduced when items are adequately controlled for phonology
(Bird, Patterson, Lambon-Ralph, McClelland & Seidenberg, 2003)

Semantic dementia patients: 
Degree of impairment with irregulars correlates strongly with severity of semantic deficit
(Patterson, Lambon-Ralph, Hodges & McClelland, 2001)

Other issues with the double dissociation data:
paragraphs: **Phonological controls can change the apparent regular–irregular difference.** Bird and colleagues found that the difference in Broca's patients was reduced when items were adequately matched for phonology.
Patterson and colleagues found that irregular impairment in semantic dementia correlated with semantic deficit severity.
These findings connect morphology to phonological and semantic abilities, making a pure rule-versus-word interpretation less straightforward.

title: Generalization and item-specific support
sourceText:
Compare this to the “triangle model” account of dyslexia:
Phonological representations support generalization.

	generalization is a result of statistical learning about patterns in the mapping from present to past

	impaired phonological representations impact these generalizations

Semantic representations support idiosyncratic forms.

	forms that deviate from the overwhelmingly regular “add –ed” pattern need support from semantics

	some “irregular” forms can take advantage of the sub-patterns, and are likely to be “spared”
paragraphs: **Phonological representations support learning the common mapping from present to past.** A degraded representation makes that generalization less reliable, especially for new words.
Semantic information supports forms that depart from the dominant -ed pattern. Some irregulars also benefit from smaller phonological families and can be relatively spared.
Regularity and exception status therefore describe degrees of statistical support rather than perfectly isolated kinds of processing.

title: Specific language impairment
sourceText:
Specific Language Impairment
Impaired language development
“Normal” performance/nonverbal IQ
Affected grammar
morphology
syntax
But also:
phonology 
reading 
working memory
speech perception
paragraphs: **Specific language impairment, or SLI in the course terminology, involves impaired language development despite relatively typical nonverbal performance.** Difficulties can include morphology and syntax.
The profile can also involve phonology, reading, working memory and speech perception. This broader range matters when evaluating a theory that locates the problem only in grammar.
A relative language difficulty does not by itself identify a single damaged learning mechanism.

title: A rule-deficit account of SLI
sourceText:
Past Tense and SLI
Past tense deficits: sine qua non of SLI
Earlier claims suggested their deficit was specific to rules
Gopnik; van der Lely; Pinker; Ullman; Clahsen
SLI could represent evidence that language acquisition requires domain-specific mechanisms
A deficit in learning rules
a problem with regulars and nonwords, but not irregulars
paragraphs: **A rule-deficit account predicts particular difficulty with regular and novel inflections.** If a domain-specific rule-learning mechanism is impaired, irregular forms stored lexically should be relatively less affected.
This proposal uses past-tense performance to argue for a mechanism specific to grammatical rules.
The prediction must be tested against the complete pattern, including irregular performance and broader phonological difficulties.

title: SLI behavioral comparison
sourceText:
Behavioral Data
van der Lely & Ullman (2001)
paragraphs: **The van der Lely and Ullman comparison shows low past-tense accuracy across all three item types in the SLI group.** Same-age controls perform much better.
Nonwords are especially difficult for the SLI group, but regulars and irregulars are also impaired. The results therefore contain a broad deficit as well as unequal condition difficulty.
An explanation should account for the entire profile rather than reporting only that productive forms are poor.

title: Developmental model results
sourceText: Model Results
paragraphs: **Weakening phonological processing produces impaired learning across forms, with nonwords especially vulnerable.** The severe and weaker impairment settings differ in the degree of difficulty.
The intact model performs substantially better. Even intact learning shows different performance across regulars, irregulars and nonwords.
The comparison tests whether a phonological learning weakness can reproduce important aspects of the behavioral profile without a missing grammatical rule.

title: Why phonology affects all forms
sourceText:
Summary
The model illustrates how phonology affects development of all forms

…and why it’s especially important to  nonwords
paragraphs: **Phonology contributes to every spoken past-tense response.** Weakening it can therefore reduce performance on regulars, irregulars and nonwords.
Nonwords are particularly dependent on generalizing a sound pattern to a new form. Familiar words have additional item-specific learning that can partly support their responses.

title: A unified learning account
sourceText:
Note similarities to “triangle” model of reading.
There are no “special rules” for the past tense, just mappings between phonology and semantics.

There is no separate lexicon that stores the exceptions.

Indeed, the concept of “rule” and “exception” only approximately describes the system.

Association between “irregular” forms and semantic processing.

Association between “wug test” performance and phonological processing.
paragraphs: **The associative account learns mappings among phonology and semantics without a separate symbolic past-tense rule or an isolated exception lexicon.** Regular and irregular are useful descriptions of behavior, but only approximate descriptions of the system's internal organization.
Irregular performance is associated with semantic processing. Wug-test performance is associated with phonological processing.
These associations provide tests of the proposed underlying mechanisms, beyond simply assigning different item types to different boxes.
