Read Borodisky (2003) on Linguistic Relativity

title: Language and thought
sourceText: Language and Thought

title: Linguistic relativity
sourceText:
“No two languages are ever sufficiently similar to be considered as representing the same 
social reality. The worlds in which different societies live are distinct worlds, not merely 
the same world with different labels attached.”
Sapir (1929)
Linguistic Relativity, a.k.a. The “Sapir-Whorf Hypothesis”
“We dissect nature along lines laid down by our native language. The categories and 
types that we isolate from the world of phenomena we do not find there because they 
stare every observer in the face; on the contrary, the world is presented in a 
kaleidoscope flux of impressions which has to be organized by our minds—and this 
means largely by the linguistic systems of our minds. We cut nature up, organize it into 
concepts, and ascribe significances as we do, largely because we are parties to an 
agreement to organize it in this way—an agreement that holds throughout our speech 
community and is codified in the patterns of our language [...] all observers are not led 
by the same physical evidence to the same picture of the universe, unless their linguistic 
backgrounds are similar, or can in some way be calibrated.”
Whorf (1956)
(The Wikipedia page on this is actually pretty useful, BTW)
paragraphs: **Linguistic relativity concerns whether differences in language influence how people organize or use concepts.** The Sapir and Whorf quotations suggest that linguistic categories can shape how experience is interpreted.
The strongest reading would make language determine what a person can think. A weaker claim is that habitual language use biases attention, memory or preferred ways of representing a situation.
These claims require different evidence. A preference associated with language does not establish that alternative thought is impossible.

title: Language, culture and the strength of the claim
sourceText:
Linguistic Relativity
Keep in mind:
Even Sapir and Whorf did not necessarily hold the “strong” relativist position implied 
in those pull-quotes.
In the first half of the 20th Century, linguistics was really part of anthropology, so 
treating language as a part of culture seemed more natural than it does to contemporary 
linguists.
We’re going to be talking mainly about space and the relationship between space and 
time.
paragraphs: **Language is embedded in cultural practices and experience.** A difference between language communities may therefore covary with factors other than linguistic structure.
Sapir and Whorf should not automatically be assigned the strongest deterministic interpretation of selected quotations.
A precise study must identify which cognitive process is affected and what alternative explanations the comparison controls.

title: Locating the ball
sourceText:
Thinking about space…
Where’s the ball?
paragraphs: **A location description needs a frame of reference.** Saying where the ball is requires choosing what counts as left, front or a stable direction.
The ball can be located with respect to the viewer, the chair's own orientation or a direction independent of either.
Different descriptions can identify the same physical position while organizing that position differently.

title: Intrinsic, relative and absolute frames
sourceText:
Thinking about space…
(Levinson et al., 2002, Cognition)
paragraphs: **An intrinsic frame uses an object's own orientation, a relative frame uses an observer's viewpoint, and an absolute frame uses a stable direction.** These are different ways to specify the same location.
“At the chair's front” uses the chair's intrinsic front. “To the left of the chair from my viewpoint” depends on the observer.
“North of the chair” uses an absolute direction that does not reverse when the observer turns around.

title: Egocentric and absolute spatial language
sourceText:
Thinking about space…
It seems natural in most languages to talk 
about space egocentrically when talking about 
things that are nearby.
What is to your left or to your right, in front of 
you or behind you, etc.
Not so in Tzeltal, a Western Mayan language 
spoken in Chiapas.
In this language (and a small number of others, 
mostly unrelated to one another, and broadly 
distributed, e.g., in Bali and Queensland) 
absolute directions are used.
Raise your east hand if this seems intuitive to 
you… 
Some native Tzeltal speakers defending their land 
from the vampire squid of neoliberalism.
paragraphs: **Egocentric spatial descriptions use the speaker's position and orientation.** Left, right, in front and behind are familiar examples for nearby objects.
Tzeltal commonly uses absolute directions in circumstances where English speakers might use these relative terms.
The contrast motivates asking whether habitual language use relates to nonverbal spatial coding, rather than merely comparing two ways of giving spoken directions.

title: Tzeltal uphill and downhill
sourceText:
Tzeltal has a historically landmark-
based system.
Things are either “uphill” or 
“downhill” from one another, not to 
the left or right of the speaker or 
interlocutor.
In fact, “uphill” and “downhill” are 
used as cardinal directions, making 
this an absolute system. 
Beautiful downtown Tenejapa.
(Levinson et al., 2002, Cognition)
paragraphs: **Tzeltal's uphill and downhill terms function as an absolute directional system.** Their historical connection to a slope does not mean that each use simply points to the nearest visible hill.
A direction is retained as a stable spatial reference rather than being recalculated from the speaker's current left and right.
This allows positions to be described consistently as the speaker changes orientation.

title: Landmark-based directions
sourceText:
New Yorkers use “uptown” 
and “downtown” as if they 
were cardinal directions all 
the time, but these don’t 
work outside of Manhattan. 
So that is literally a landmark-
based system.
Also, the subway map really 
has us messed up on “north” 
and “south,” because 
Manhattan is on an angle 
w/r/t magnetic north.
An aside
paragraphs: **A landmark-based direction is tied to a particular environment.** Uptown and downtown organize movement within Manhattan but do not provide a universally usable compass system.
A city's conventional map orientation can also differ from magnetic north. Familiar spatial language therefore reflects local practices as well as geometric directions.

title: The rotated spatial-memory task
sourceText:
Majid et al. (2004, TiCS)
A non-linguistic test for relative vs. absolute coding of space
paragraphs: **The chips task separates relative from absolute spatial memory by rotating the participant 180 degrees.** A participant sees a configuration, waits, and then chooses its match at a second table.
A relative response preserves the arrangement with respect to the person's viewpoint. An absolute response preserves its orientation in the environment, so the two responses diverge after rotation.

Dutch speakers predominantly gave relative responses, while Tzeltal speakers gave more absolute responses. The association is consistent with their preferred linguistic frames but does not isolate language from all other experience.

title: Spatial inference across displays
sourceText:
Majid et al. (2004, TiCS)
You can get really fancy with this.
paragraphs: **Spatial inference can combine relations learned in different displays.** Participants learn the relation between two objects, rotate to another display, and learn a second relation involving a shared object.
They then place an object relative to another using the combined information. Relative and absolute coding lead to different placements because the person's orientation has changed.
Dutch and Tzeltal response patterns again differ in the direction associated with their preferred spatial frames.

title: A testing-environment alternative
sourceText:
Li and Gleitman:
Inducing landmark-based similarity in English speakers 
Consider the conditions under which 
the Tzeltal speakers were tested: 
Outside, with visible, familiar landmarks. 
Typical psychology lab studies are done 
in windowless rooms.
paragraphs: **Testing conditions could contribute to the apparent language-group difference.** Li and Gleitman noted that Tzeltal participants had been tested with visible, familiar outdoor landmarks, unlike many laboratory participants.
An environment with useful landmarks can encourage landmark-based coding. A windowless laboratory can make viewer-relative descriptions more convenient.
Manipulating landmark availability within English speakers tests whether the behavior can change without changing native language.

title: Blinds down, blinds up and outdoors
sourceText:
In the “blinds down” condition, English 
speakers overwhelmingly use relative position 
in this task – like the Dutch speakers in prior 
studies.
With the blinds up and a view of the street, or 
outdoors, their preference is less pronounced. 
Li and Gleitman:
Inducing landmark-based spatial reasoning in English 
speakers
paragraphs: **English speakers' preference for relative coding weakened when external landmarks were available.** They strongly preferred relative responses with the blinds down, but the preference was less pronounced with a street view or outdoors.
The manipulation changes the spatial information available while keeping the language group the same.
This demonstrates that task context can influence the response. It challenges an explanation in which language alone fixes the chosen frame.

title: Discussion pause
sourceText: What does it mean?

title: What the environmental confound means
sourceText:
What does it mean?
What if the differences between language groups are confounded with differences in 
testing conditions?
Maybe the bias toward relative spatial reasoning is an artifact of the way psychology 
tests are typically run in universities…
paragraphs: **If language groups are tested under different conditions, their response difference may partly reflect those conditions.** Visible landmarks and familiarity can covary with native language in a cross-community study.
A controlled comparison must separate the effect of the environment from any contribution of habitual linguistic coding.
Showing an environmental effect does not prove that language never matters. It limits what can be inferred from an uncontrolled comparison.

title: Levinson's methodological response
sourceText:
Levinson and colleagues 
were not impressed.
They claim that Li and 
Gleitman made it too 
transparent that they were 
testing something to do 
with rotation by reducing 
memory load and 
time/distance between 
stimulus and test.
Also Li and Gleitman’s
participants were Ivy 
League students, who excel 
at figuring out what the 
professor wants and then 
making it happen.
paragraphs: **Levinson and colleagues argued that the simplified task could make the experimenter's purpose too obvious.** Low memory demands and short time or distance between displays may encourage a deliberate strategy about rotation.
Participants who infer what is being tested can alter their response for reasons different from habitual spatial coding.
The response therefore focuses on memory load and task transparency, rather than denying that landmarks can ever matter.

title: Increasing memory load and reducing transparency
sourceText:
Levinson et al. (2002) re-ran the “animals in a row” experiment with Dutch college 
students, but including a fourth animal, a longer delay interval (both to increase memory 
load) and a larger distance between the stimulus and response tables (to reduce the 
salience of the rotation).
Under these conditions, a bias to use relative framing remains.
paragraphs: **Levinson and colleagues retested Dutch students with four animals, a longer delay and greater distance between tables.** The extra item and delay increased memory demands, while the distance made the rotation manipulation less conspicuous.
Under these conditions, the preference for relative coding remained.
The result suggests that the environmental effect depends on how the task is arranged, including how much memory and strategic inference it encourages.

title: Memory as part of the explanation
sourceText:
What does it mean?
For speakers of languages that use relative spatial frames of reference, the bias to use 
relative vs. absolute frames is robust to the environment when:
1. There’s a significant memory component, and
2. The experimenter’s interest in rotation and frames of reference isn’t obvious
Can you think of a way in which the importance of “memory” muddies the waters here?
paragraphs: **A robust spatial-frame preference under memory demands does not automatically identify a purely spatial representation.** Remembering the task can recruit verbal strategies as well as spatial ones.
The relative preference is reported when memory demands are substantial and the experimenter's interest is less obvious.
That pattern makes it important to ask how the sequence is stored during the delay, not only which direction is chosen at the end.

title: Verbal recoding of a spatial sequence
sourceText:
What does it mean?
For speakers of languages that use relative spatial frames of reference, the bias to use 
relative vs. absolute frames is robust to the environment when:
1. There’s a significant memory component, and
2. The experimenter’s interest in rotation and frames of reference isn’t obvious
Can you think of a way in which the importance of “memory” muddies the waters here? 
What if participants are just recoding the list in working memory as a sequence, e.g. “lion, 
tiger, bear,” and then naturally working from left to right?
Why does “left to right” seem like a natural translation of a temporal sequence?
paragraphs: **Participants might remember the animals as a verbal list such as “lion, tiger, bear.”** Reconstructing that sequence from left to right can produce a relative-looking response.
This strategy would connect language to the task through working memory and ordering habits, rather than through an inability to represent absolute space.
The interpretation changes because the same choice can arise from different internal codes.

title: Metaphor and abstract concepts
sourceText:
“You’re like a dull knife.
Just ain’t cuttin’.
Because you’re talkin’ loud,
But you ain’t sayin’ nothin’.
(Brown & Byrd, 1970)
Metaphorical language and “abstract” concepts.
What’s going on here?
How is failing to make a compelling argument 
like “not cutting?”
Do you literally have to be speaking in a loud 
voice to be “talking loud” but “saying 
nothing?”
Obviously, James Brown was a great artist, so we expect him to use evocative language. 
But how much of language can we safely describe as non-metaphorical?
What is the point here? 
Is the discussion of Language and Thought a knotty and convoluted argument that 
generates more heat than light. In the following section, we’ll pursue the problem of 
whether language has an impact on how we think about time in terms of space.
paragraphs: **Metaphorical language expresses one kind of experience using terms from another.** Saying that an argument is not “cutting” describes its effectiveness rather than a literal action with a blade.
Physical and spatial terms can therefore help express abstract relations. Time is especially useful for studying whether such linguistic habits are associated with nonlinguistic representations.
The question is empirical. Using a spatial phrase does not by itself prove that every thought about time has the same spatial format.

title: Spatial language for time
sourceText:
Spatial metaphors for time in different languages
(Boroditsky et al., 2010)
paragraphs: **English and Mandarin both use horizontal spatial language for time, but Mandarin also frequently uses vertical terms.** Earlier events can be described with an “up” term and later events with a “down” term.
The linguistic contrast motivates testing whether speakers differ in the spatial organization they use during temporal tasks.
The existence of the expressions is the starting observation. A behavioral task is needed to investigate whether the contrast extends beyond words.

title: Spatial priming and temporal judgments
sourceText:
Boroditsky, 2001)
A priming experiment
Priming with a spatial task (horizontal or vertical) has different effects on temporal 
processing in the two languages.
Short-term training on vertical metaphors for time (“Cars were invented above fax 
machines”) also has an impact.
paragraphs: **Boroditsky's priming task tests whether spatial processing influences subsequent time judgments.** Participants first process horizontal or vertical relations, then respond to temporal earlier–later questions.
English speakers respond faster after horizontal than vertical primes, while Mandarin speakers show the opposite pattern in the displayed comparison.

Training English speakers on vertical metaphors changes the pattern toward a vertical-prime advantage. This suggests sensitivity to experience, rather than an unchangeable division between language groups.

title: Reading direction as an alternative
sourceText:
Casasanto & Bottini (2005, Cognitive Science Proceedings)
An alternative explanation: direction of text…
paragraphs: **Reading and writing habits can also organize sequences spatially.** Differences attributed to temporal metaphors may covary with whether text is commonly read left-to-right, right-to-left or vertically.
Casasanto and Bottini use differences in text orientation and arrangement preferences to motivate this alternative.
The point is to identify another source of spatial experience, not to assume that a writing-system label perfectly predicts every individual's habits.

title: Controlling reported vertical reading
sourceText:
Boroditsky et al. (2010, Cognition)
Excluding Chinese readers who reported 
reading top-to-bottom. 
…so Boroditsky et al. controlled for that…
paragraphs: **Boroditsky and colleagues excluded Chinese readers who reported top-to-bottom reading.** This tests whether the vertical temporal effect can be explained entirely by that reported reading experience.
English speakers show an advantage for a left-is-earlier horizontal mapping. Mandarin speakers also show an advantage for a top-is-earlier vertical mapping in the displayed comparison.
Retaining a vertical effect under this restriction weakens that particular reading-direction explanation, without proving that every possible experiential confound is removed.

title: Past–future button mappings
sourceText:
Casasanto & Bottini (2010, Spatial Cognition)
Task: Push a blue button for events in the past, a red button for events in the future 
(or the reverse, in different blocks). 
Thus, half the time, the “past” is on the left, and the other half it’s on the right.
paragraphs: **Participants classify events as past or future using colored buttons.** The color-to-category mapping is reversed across blocks, so the past response is sometimes on the left and sometimes on the right.
With standard text reading, responses are faster when past maps left and future maps right.
Because the response concerns time rather than an explicit judgment of spatial direction, the compatibility effect reveals an implicit spatial association in this task.

title: Mirror reading changes the mapping effect
sourceText:
Casasanto & Bottini (2010, Spatial Cognition)
Task: Push a blue button for events in the past, a red button for events in the future 
(or the reverse, in different blocks). 
Thus, half the time, the “past” is on the left, and the other half it’s on the right. 
Now ask people to do a few minutes of 
“mirror reading:”
paragraphs: **Mirror reading tests whether short-term reading experience can alter spatial associations with time.** Participants read reversed text and perform the past–future button task.
By the second mirror-reading block, the compatibility effect reverses. Responses are faster when earlier maps right and later maps left.
The result supports a contribution of reading-direction experience and shows that the association can change over a short period.

title: Evaluating vocabulary anecdotes
sourceText:
(for those of you who were straining your eyes to read this on the last slide, it’s from a classic rant by 
Pullum (1989, Natural Language and Linguistic Theory) called “The Great *Eskimo Vocabulary Hoax.” 
See if you can guess where he comes down on linguistic relativism…) 
*not an OK word for Inuktitut people whose language is the most likely source for the examples, but 
it’s the title of the book, sorry 
paragraphs: **Claims about a language's vocabulary are not automatically evidence for cognitive limits.** Pullum's discussion criticizes how an account of different word roots became an exaggerated story about language and thought.
Languages can express distinctions through separate roots, derived words or phrases. Counting one of these forms without considering the others can misrepresent expressive capacity.
A reliable claim requires accurate linguistic description and an appropriate behavioral test, rather than repetition of a striking anecdote.

title: Reading assignment
sourceText:
For next week: Bavelier et al. on cortical plasticity 
http://www.nature.com/nrn/journal/v3/n6/abs/nrn848.html

title: Language in different modalities
sourceText:
Language in different modalities: 
Sign and Braille

title: Signed languages and Braille
sourceText:
Note
Sign language and Braille are really different cases.
Sign languages, as we’ll see, are natural languages that have their own linguistic 
structure.
Braille is a system that allows blind individuals to read a spoken language they share with 
sighted individuals.
I’ve lumped them together because they reveal interesting things about the plasticity of 
sensory systems, and how the brain gets organized differently when language input 
comes from different modalities.
paragraphs: **A signed language is a natural language, while Braille is a writing system.** Signed languages have their own linguistic structure. Braille allows a language to be read through touch.
The distinction matters because changing the modality of a language is not the same as changing how a written language is accessed.
Both cases reveal how sensory experience shapes the organization of systems involved in language and reading.

title: How signed languages differ from speech
sourceText:
Sign Language
Emmorey et al. (2004, Brain & Language)
Sign languages have some obvious differences 
from spoken languages:
- modality
- articulators
- use of space
- iconicity (though this is easy to exaggerate 
when you look at individual words with their 
glosses)
paragraphs: **Signed languages use a visual modality and manual and bodily articulators.** The hands, face and upper body contribute to a coordinated linguistic signal.
Space can carry linguistic relations. Some signs are iconic, meaning that aspects of their form resemble aspects of their meaning.
Iconicity is easy to overestimate when a familiar translation is supplied. A visible resemblance does not eliminate the need to learn a language's forms and structure.

title: Coordinated signing
sourceText:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8J_UfLH8isU
Note:
- eye contact
- coordination of hands, face, upper body
- fluidity (can you segment words?)
- speed 
Take a look at sign language in action.
paragraphs: **Fluent signing coordinates hands, facial expression, gaze and upper-body movement.** The linguistic signal is distributed across these visible articulators rather than produced by one hand movement at a time.
Like speech, a fluent stream is continuous enough that word boundaries are not always obvious to a learner.
Eye contact and movement timing are therefore relevant to perceiving the interaction, alongside the form of individual signs.

title: Contrastive features in sign
sourceText:
As with speech, there are featural descriptions of sign. 
Signs can differ contrastively in:
- hand configuration
- gesture location
- movement    
(Emmorey et al., 2003, Language & Cognitive Processes)
Phonology of sign language.
“please”
“sorry”
“onion”
“apple”
paragraphs: **Signed-language phonology includes contrastive hand configuration, location and movement.** Changing one of these features can distinguish signs, just as changing a speech feature can distinguish spoken words.
The PLEASE–SORRY and ONION–APPLE examples demonstrate that closely related visible forms can have different linguistic identities.
Phonology therefore concerns the organization of contrastive form, not only acoustic sound.

title: Testing categorical perception in sign
sourceText: Research question: Is there categorical perception for these dimensions?
paragraphs: **Categorical perception can be tested by varying a sign feature continuously.** The hand-configuration continuum moves between forms while the observer's identification and discrimination responses are measured.
One continuum crosses a phonemic distinction between PLEASE and SORRY. The allophonic comparison varies hand configuration without the same change in sign identity.
A sharp identification boundary accompanied by better discrimination near that boundary would indicate category-sensitive perception.

title: Identification and discrimination results
sourceText:
These curves should look 
familiar.
There is a fairly sharp
categorical boundary between 
stimuli 4 and 6 for the 
phonemic boundary. 
This corresponds to the peak in 
the discrimination function.
For the allophonic condition, 
the identification function is 
much shallower – i.e., many 
more ambiguous stimuli – and 
there is no peak in the 
discrimination function.
paragraphs: **Deaf signers show a sharper categorical boundary for phonemic than allophonic hand-configuration changes.** In the phonemic condition, identification shifts steeply around stimuli 4–6.
Discrimination is also strongest near the phonemic boundary. Comparable physical steps are easier to distinguish when they cross that category boundary.
The allophonic identification function is shallower and lacks the same localized discrimination peak. This links the perceptual pattern to linguistic contrast rather than any visible hand change.

title: Spatial information in grammar
sourceText:
Use of spatial information in grammar.
Sign language uses space to indicate relationships between words in a sentence. 
This is a very transparent example, where the relative position of two objects is given by 
where the classifier sign is made. 
Consider that understanding sentences of any complexity in sign language requires 
keeping track of where signs were made.
paragraphs: **Signed languages can use positions in signing space to represent relationships.** A classifier sign made at a particular location can indicate the relative position of an object.
Understanding a sentence can require retaining where entities were introduced and how subsequent signs relate to those locations.
Spatial processing therefore contributes to linguistic comprehension, rather than functioning only as background vision.

title: Shared and modality-related brain activity
sourceText:
Brain activity during sign language comprehension has both important 
similarities and differences with spoken language.
Similar: 
- left lateralization
- classical language areas 
(Broca’s / inferior frontal; Wernicke’s
/ posterior superior temporal)
Different:
- visual areas
- superior parietal / classic 
spatial areas
Campbell, MacSweeney, & Waters (2008)
Deaf signers
Hearing signers
Audio-visual 
Speech (hearing participants)
paragraphs: **Signed-language comprehension recruits classical language regions and shows left lateralization, as spoken-language comprehension does.** Inferior frontal and posterior superior temporal regions are part of this overlap.
Signing also engages visual and superior parietal regions relevant to its perceptual and spatial demands.
The combination suggests both common language organization and modality-related contributions. Similarity does not require identical activation everywhere.

title: Deafness, signing and peripheral attention
sourceText:
Bavelier D et al. J. Neurosci. 2001;21:8931-8942
Research question: 
Does deafness and/or experience with sign impact spatial attention?
Participants monitored for brief changes in either 
luminance or velocity of “dots” either in the center 
of the screen, or at the periphery.
Deaf participants show an advantage in this task 
when attention is directed to the periphery.
paragraphs: **Bavelier and colleagues compared hearing controls, deaf signers and hearing signers on visual attention.** Participants monitored dots for brief changes in luminance or velocity, with attention directed centrally or peripherally.
Deaf participants showed an advantage when attention was directed to the periphery.
Including hearing signers helps separate experience with signing from lack of auditory input. If all signers had the same advantage, signing alone would be a stronger explanation.

title: Two different effects of experience
sourceText:
Learning sign language changes the laterality of 
areas involved in motion perception from right to 
left.
(Perhaps because motion perception needs to 
“talk to” left-lateralized language networks in 
people who learn sign.) 
Enhancements of peripheral visual attention, 
however, are only observed in deaf individuals.
(Perhaps because hearing individuals are more 
dependent on auditory cues for spatial 
attention when things are at the far 
periphery.)
paragraphs: **Signing experience and deafness show different associations with visual processing.** Both deaf and hearing signers show a leftward shift in motion-processing lateralization relative to hearing nonsigners.
Enhanced peripheral attention is found in deaf individuals, not hearing signers. Signing experience alone therefore does not explain that enhancement.
The proposed interpretations involve links between motion and language systems for signing, and reduced reliance on auditory peripheral cues in deafness.

title: Sign language versus tic-tac gestures
sourceText:
Dissociating visual/spatial/motor processing of hand movements from language processing.
Direct comparison of sign comprehension with “tic-tac,” a sophisticated (and 
outmoded) gestural system used to communicate about odds at horse races in the 
UK.
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YsZu_wZa-j8
paragraphs: **Comparing sign comprehension with another organized gesture system helps control visible movement demands.** Tic-tac uses sophisticated hand gestures to communicate horse-racing odds.
Both tasks involve meaningful, sequenced hand movements. A difference between them is more informative about linguistic processing than a comparison between signing and no movement.
The control is not identical to a natural language, which is precisely why the remaining difference is of interest.

title: Neural difference between sign and gesture
sourceText:
D
Campbell, MacSweeney, & Waters (2008)
Stronger activity was observed around 
Wernicke’s area for sign language vs. tic-tac.
(The frontal activation is superior to Broca’s
area; you can make up a “hand-wavy” story 
about why tic-tac might activate Broca’s area.)
(See what I did there? Hand-wavy? Ha ha.)
paragraphs: **Sign language produces stronger activity around posterior superior temporal language regions than tic-tac gestures.** This supports a distinction between processing organized hand movements and processing a natural language.
The comparison reduces a simple explanation based only on the presence of hands moving through space.
The frontal activation shown is superior to classic Broca's area, so it should not be casually relabeled as a precise Broca's effect.

title: Evidence about signed language
sourceText:
So, sign language…
Sign language has phonological structure, and native speakers show categorical perception 
for some contrastive features.
Learning a signed language results in some brain reorganization, particularly the 
lateralization of motion processing.
Although attention to the visual periphery is critical for both hearing and deaf signers, only 
deaf signers show enhanced processing of visual attention in the periphery.
Compared with non-language stimuli that also involve organized, sequenced hand 
movements, signed sentences activate posterior STG (Wernicke’s area).
paragraphs: **Signed languages have linguistic form, grammar and language-related neural organization.** Contrastive sign features can produce categorical perception, and comprehension recruits posterior superior temporal language regions.
Signing experience is associated with changes in motion lateralization. Deafness is associated with enhanced peripheral attention in the reported comparison.
These findings jointly show that linguistic experience and sensory history contribute in different ways.

title: Perspective in signed spatial descriptions
paragraphs: **Comprehending a signed spatial description can require a perspective transformation.** A room can be described from the speaker's perspective or the addressee's perspective.
The figure's caption reports better comprehension for descriptions from the speaker's perspective despite the mental transformation that this requires.
This illustrates that the most linguistically natural representation is not necessarily the one that eliminates every spatial transformation.

title: Braille as tactile reading
sourceText:
Tactile reading: Braille
Braille reading is in many ways equivalent to reading print, BUT:
- symbols are optimized for tactile discrimination (reading Braille by sight is really hard)
- fingers take in letters one at a time
paragraphs: **Braille represents written language through tactilely distinguishable symbols.** It is a way to read a language, rather than a separate natural language with its own grammar.
The symbols are optimized for touch. Fingers acquire letters sequentially, creating perceptual demands that differ from viewing printed text.
The comparison asks how reading networks operate when the input arrives through touch instead of vision.

title: Blindness onset and visual-cortex recruitment
sourceText:
Reading Braille activates visual cortex 
in blind individuals.
The images on the left show three 
early blind participants, with late blind 
participants on the right.
The earlier sight is lost, the more 
extensive visual activity is to tactile 
stimuli.
We haven’t talked about the “visual 
word form area,” but it’s strongly 
activated in early blind participants, 
more so than late blind.
paragraphs: **Braille reading activates visual cortex in blind individuals, with more extensive recruitment after earlier sight loss.** Early- and late-blind groups therefore provide a comparison of developmental sensory history.
Early-blind participants show stronger involvement of regions associated with visual word processing than late-blind participants.
This indicates that a region's usual sensory label does not completely determine the information it can help process.

title: Five days of blindfolding
sourceText:
A question about competition
Remember that we worried about 
whether competition could be 
preventing hearing individuals from 
developing awesome peripheral 
visual attention?
Merabet et al. asked sighted 
individuals to wear blindfolds for five 
days, and trained them to read 
Braille.
Relative to a control group, the 
blindfolded group learned more 
quickly.  
Merabet et al. (2008, PLoS ONE)
paragraphs: **Merabet and colleagues tested rapid plasticity by blindfolding sighted adults for five days while training Braille.** A comparison group received training without the same continuous removal of visual input.
The blindfolded group learned more quickly. This suggests that eliminating competing visual input can affect tactile learning over a short timescale.
Because the participants were sighted adults, the experiment tests a different question from lifelong or early blindness.

title: Rapid and reversible recruitment
sourceText:
Merabet LB, Hamilton R, Schlaug G, Swisher JD, et al. (2008) Rapid and Reversible Recruitment of Early Visual Cortex for Touch. PLoS ONE 3(8): 
e3046. doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0003046
http://www.plosone.org/article/info:doi/10.1371/journal.pone.0003046
Further, over the course of the experiment, 
sighted, blindfolded participants started to 
show some activity in primary visual cortex 
when reading Braille.
When the blindfold was removed on Day 6, 
the effect was completely reversed.
paragraphs: **Visual-cortex responses to Braille developed during blindfolding and reversed after the blindfold was removed on Day 6.** The time course shows that the change was rapid and reversible.
Removing visual input can allow tactile-related activity to become more evident. Restoring vision changes that balance again.
This pattern is consistent with unmasking existing inputs rather than requiring the creation of an entirely new pathway over a few days.

title: TMS tests functional contribution
sourceText:
When transcranial magnetic 
stimulation (TMS) was used to 
disrupt activity in visual cortex, 
it disrupted reading in the 
blindfolded group only (solid 
symbols).
This is evidence that the 
blindfolded participants are 
somehow using visual cortex
for tactile processing. (Maybe?)
One way to think about this is that visual cortex is getting tactile 
input all the time, even in sighted, unblindfolded people, but that 
this input is too weak to compete with the much stronger, more 
consistent visual input.
Even short-term removal of visual input can “unmask” tactile 
responses in visual cortex.
paragraphs: **Disrupting visual cortex with TMS impaired Braille discrimination in the blindfolded group.** This goes beyond showing that the region becomes active during touch.
On Day 5, the blindfolded group's error rate rises under 1 Hz TMS relative to its baseline and sham conditions. The nonblindfolded group does not show the same selective disruption.
The effect is no longer present in the same way after blindfold removal. The result supports a temporary functional contribution of visual cortex to tactile performance.

title: Cross-modal plasticity and language
sourceText:
Cross-modal plasticity and language
An important point is the resilience of language circuitry despite differences in modality. 
- Classical language areas are activated by sign language, although the input is 
dramatically different in its surface form.
- Braille reading seems to engage networks that are important for processing text.
We can think of cross-modal plasticity as demonstrating that brain organization is shaped 
over the course of development by competition.
For example, when auditory input is unavailable, putative auditory areas are used to 
process sign, and visual attention is enhanced at the periphery.
Recall that the competing cognitive/perceptual processes shaping language processing 
were also important when we considered the Competition Model as relevant to second 
language learning.
paragraphs: **Language-related organization is resilient across sensory modalities while remaining shaped by experience.** Signed language recruits classical language regions, and Braille engages networks associated with text processing.
Competition among available inputs offers a way to understand reorganization. When an input is absent or reduced, other information can make a larger contribution.
The evidence does not imply that all regions are interchangeable. It shows both stable functional relationships and experience-sensitive recruitment.

title: Final review
sourceText: Review Session

title: Orthographic depth
sourceText:
We were able to demonstrate that 
phonemes are not letters, but also 
that letters are not phonemes with 
a “mispronouncing contest” in 
which people willfully 
mispronounced words like:
COLONEL
PARADIGM
We also talked about how some 
scripts (like Pinyin for Mandarin 
and French) are relatively regular.
This difference between scripts is also referred to as orthographic depth. 
English, due its irregularities is a relatively deep script. 
Finnish and Korean are very shallow scripts.
paragraphs: **Orthographic depth** describes how consistently spelling corresponds to pronunciation. English is relatively deep because many spellings do not transparently specify their sounds.
COLONEL and PARADIGM make the problem concrete. Applying common letter–sound patterns can produce a plausible-looking pronunciation that is wrong for the actual word.

In shallower writing systems, such as Finnish and Korean, spelling–sound correspondences are more predictable. The comparison concerns the writing system, not the intelligence or ability of its readers.

title: Transparent spelling in Finnish
sourceText:
Some writing systems, like Finnish, are 
very “transparent” (or “shallow” 
according to the Orthographic Depth 
Hypothesis).
Let’s listen to this beginning Finnish 
lesson and follow along with the text…
After about a minute of this, you 
probably get the idea?
Each letter corresponds more or less 
unambiguously to one phoneme. 
Doubled letters actually correspond to 
geminated consonants or long vowels.
Finnish children learn to decode
pronunciations for written forms very 
very quickly. 
http://tasteoffinnish.fi/lesson1-1/
paragraphs: **Finnish has a shallow orthography.** Letters correspond relatively unambiguously to phonemes, so learning a spelling–sound correspondence helps with many different words.
Doubled letters represent a meaningful length distinction. A doubled consonant is geminated, and a doubled vowel is long.
This regularity helps Finnish children learn decoding quickly. Decoding means generating a pronunciation from a written form, whether or not its meaning is familiar.

title: Learning to decode across languages
sourceText:
In fact, English is a bit of an outlier 
among languages that use the Roman 
alphabet. 
One result is that kids learn to decode 
more slowly in English.
In Grade 1, kids learning a wide variety 
of other languages are able to generate 
plausible pronunciations for 
“pseudowords,” (made up words that 
follow the spelling and sound patterns 
of their language) at a much higher rate 
than English learners.
paragraphs: **Pseudoword reading tests decoding.** Because a pseudoword is not a familiar stored word, the child must generalize from learned spelling–sound patterns.

The comparison involves Grade 1 children learning different alphabetic writing systems. Children learning many other languages produce plausible pseudoword pronunciations more successfully than English learners.
English's less predictable correspondences help explain why decoding develops more slowly. This task does not measure the child's entire language ability.

title: Korean letter forms and sounds
sourceText:
Korean is even more regular than 
Finnish!
The symbols for similar phonemes 
are represented as similar to one 
another. 
What orthographic feature 
corresponds roughly to velar place of 
articulation, for example?
paragraphs: **Korean writing represents sound structure systematically.** Related phonemes can have related written shapes, so the visual forms themselves reflect aspects of phonological organization.
The letters are arranged into syllable blocks with initial, medial and sometimes final positions. Those positions are not three unrelated pictures of whole words.
The velar consonant forms share the basic angular ㄱ shape. Additional strokes or doubling distinguish related consonants.

title: Frequency by regularity interaction
sourceText:
This is a landmark finding in psycholinguistics. 
We’ll see how it has impacted a number of other areas 
(most immediately inflectional morphology).
What does it mean?
The frequency effect is much 
larger for exception words 
than regular words. 
Behold: The Frequency by Regularity interaction.
paragraphs: **Frequency and regularity interact.** Low-frequency exception words are slowed much more than low-frequency regular words, whereas high-frequency words show a much smaller regularity difference.
Naming latency is the time needed to begin saying the word. Higher values mean slower responses.
An interaction means the effect of one factor depends on the other. The regularity cost is not a fixed amount added equally to high- and low-frequency words.

title: Dual-route interpretation of the interaction
sourceText:
One interpretation
There are two separate processes in word recognition: 
1. A sublexical process (decoding), and
2. A lexical process (knowledge of a particular word)
For high frequency (HF) words, the lexical process is so fast and efficient that there is little 
influence of the sublexical process.
The sublexical process only shows up when we read nonwords, or low frequency (LF) words.
paragraphs: **A dual-route interpretation separates lexical retrieval from sublexical decoding.** The lexical process supplies the learned pronunciation of a particular word, while decoding computes pronunciation from spelling units.
For a high-frequency word, lexical information becomes available quickly enough to reduce the influence of the decoding output.
For a low-frequency exception, the lexical response is less efficient and the regularized decoding output can interfere. Nonwords depend on decoding because they lack a stored whole-word entry.

title: Distributed knowledge and general learning
sourceText:
PDP models of visual word recognition
Seidenberg & McClelland (1989)
Different assumptions from dual-route models:
- “rules” are just generalizations from lots of 
words, not a separate process
- the “lexicon” is also distributed. Some 
whole-word information is stored in O P 
mappings, some in  other parts of the system.
Different research strategy from dual-route 
models:
Explain reading in terms of domain-general 
learning mechanisms, rather than reverse-
engineer the system from adult/neuropsych data.
paragraphs: **In a PDP account, rules are generalizations learned across words.** Whole-word knowledge is distributed across learned mappings instead of being stored only in a distinct lexical route.
The same learning mechanism can capture both patterns shared by many words and information specific to a familiar word.
The research strategy asks whether domain-general learning can explain reading. This contrasts with choosing separate adult processing components primarily from neuropsychological dissociations.

title: Learning the frequency–regularity interaction
sourceText:
Frequency by regularity interaction
The model captured the interaction between 
frequency and regularity without assuming 
that these effects resulted from different 
processes.
How?
- “regular” words are consistent with 
statistical patterns from many other words.
- “exception” words are inconsistent with 
these statistics.
- frequency also impacts how well words 
are learned. So, highly frequent words are 
less effected by inconsistency with other 
words.
paragraphs: **A learned network can produce a frequency-by-regularity interaction without separate frequency and rule mechanisms.** Regular words receive support from patterns shared across many words.
An exception conflicts with those patterns, so learning its particular mapping is especially important. Frequent exposure strengthens that word-specific mapping.
A low-frequency exception has both weak item-specific learning and poor support from the dominant pattern. This combination creates a larger disadvantage than either factor alone.

title: Using learned weights for nonwords
sourceText:
Reading words and nonwords in the same 
“route”
In principle: 
- nonwords named via the same set of weights used 
for words.
- generalization takes advantage of the same statistical 
patterns that give rise to regularity effects.
paragraphs: **A PDP model can pronounce nonwords using the weights learned from real words.** A new spelling activates patterns that overlap with familiar spellings, allowing the network to generalize.
No stored entry for the particular nonword is required. The same learned correspondences that support consistent words can support a new combination.
This is a proposed mechanism for decoding without a separate GPC rule module.

title: Theory versus implementation
sourceText:
In practice, though, not so great…
Nonword accuracy was not very 
good.
Why?
This is a classic case of ambiguity in 
model evaluation.
Was the theoretical claim -- that 
nonwords and exceptions could 
be read by the same, associative 
mechanism – wrong?
Or, was the problem something 
specific to the way the model was 
made?
paragraphs: **Poor nonword performance can challenge either a theoretical proposal or a particular implementation.** The early model's nonword accuracy was weaker than desired.
One possibility is that a single associative mechanism cannot explain the task. Another is that the chosen representations fail to capture the similarities needed for generalization.
Improving the implementation while retaining the theoretical mechanism helps distinguish these possibilities.

title: Phonological representation matters
sourceText:
Nonword reading related to phonological representations
Many studies demonstrate a 
relationship between “decoding” 
(i.e., nonword reading) and 
phonological processing.
The phonological representations 
used in Seidenberg & McClelland 
were sort of weird:  Wickelfeatures.
Indeed, a model by Plaut et al. (1996, 
Psych Review) improved the 
phonological representations, and 
produced better performance on 
nonwords.
paragraphs: **Generalization depends on how sound similarity is represented.** The early Seidenberg–McClelland model used Wickelfeatures, whose representation of phonology was problematic for nonword reading.
Plaut and colleagues improved the phonological representations and obtained better nonword performance. This supports a representational explanation for at least part of the earlier failure.
Behavioral relations between phonological processing and decoding also make phonology a relevant target for explanation.

title: Why degraded phonology hurts generalization
sourceText:
How are phonological representations and 
nonword generalization related?
Generalization depends on similarity. (In fact this principle is 
inherited from behaviorism.)
Poor phonological representations (like Wickelfeatures) fail to 
adequately capture the similarity space of words in the language.
Word-specific information is more robust to poor representations, 
because it doesn’t depend entirely on generalization.
paragraphs: **A network generalizes through similarity.** If its phonological representation poorly captures similarities among words, the learned mapping cannot transfer as effectively to new forms.
A familiar word can retain support from its own training history. A nonword lacks that item-specific experience and depends more heavily on generalization.
This produces a reason for unfamiliar forms to be especially vulnerable to poor representations without requiring a dedicated nonword mechanism.

title: Harm and Seidenberg's noise manipulation
sourceText:
How are phonological representations and 
nonword generalization related?
Harm & Seidenberg (1999) investigated 
this more systematically, by 
manipulating the amount of “noise” in 
the phonological representations.
They were able to replicate a number of 
key findings in the literature on 
developmental dyslexia:
- relationship between degree of 
phonological deficit and phonological 
dyslexia
- relative sparing of word recognition
paragraphs: **Harm and Seidenberg manipulated noise in phonological representations.** Increasing noise makes the sound representations less reliable while keeping the model's general learning framework.
The manipulation produced poorer nonword decoding and relative sparing of word recognition. It also linked the severity of the phonological deficit to the degree of decoding difficulty.
The model therefore connects a reading pattern to the quality of a more general phonological system.

title: A dual-process past-tense architecture
sourceText:
A “dual route” model for the past tense
Pinker & Ullman (2002, TICS)
How is this similar to the dual-route model we 
were just considering for reading?
How is it different?
paragraphs: **The lexicon and grammar offer different ways to produce a past tense.** Lexical retrieval supplies an irregular form such as HELD, while grammatical combination can produce WALK plus -ed.
Pinker and Ullman's diagram associates lexical lookup with declarative memory and grammatical combination with procedural processing.

Like dual-route reading, the account separates word-specific knowledge from a productive operation. Unlike reading aloud, its task is to transform a stem according to a grammatical feature, rather than convert spelling into sound.

title: Why separate rules from exceptions?
sourceText:
Similar architecture, different origins
Remember the dual route model was 
developed based on 
neuropsychological double-
dissociations.
Pinker et al. are motivated by other 
concerns.
Generative linguistics of the time was 
mostly about categorical, symbolic, 
rule-based grammars.
These rules often have exceptions.
paragraphs: **The Words and Rules proposal was motivated partly by a theory of grammar.** A categorical symbolic grammar describes productive patterns, but language also contains exceptions.

Reading dual-route theories were strongly motivated by neuropsychological dissociations. The morphology proposal also reflects a commitment to keeping the grammatical rule system distinct from exceptional lexical information.

title: Properties of the exception system
sourceText:
Similar architecture, different origins
Rather than make the grammar inelegant by 
adding machinery to handle the 
exceptions, linguists would often just 
leave the exceptions out of the grammar.
So dual-process model proposes a way to 
“handle” the exceptions while keeping 
the grammar elegant, symbolic, 
categorical, etc.
This second process had all the properties 
the rule route did not. It was:
- word-specific (lexical)
- sensitive to frequency of occurrence
- sensitive to phonological similarity 
(keep-kept, weep-wept, leap-leapt, etc.)
paragraphs: **An associative lexicon handles information that does not fit a categorical rule.** Its representations are word-specific and sensitive to frequency and phonological similarity.
KEEP–KEPT, WEEP–WEPT and LEAP–LEAPT illustrate similarity among irregular forms. An exception can belong to a small family rather than being wholly unrelated to other words.
Assigning these properties to lexical memory lets the rule system remain categorical and general.

title: An associative alternative
sourceText:
An alternative approach: It’s all 
associative learning!
Rumelhart & McClelland (1987) available, along with lots of these other papers, here: 
http://psych.stanford.edu/~jlm/papers/
paragraphs: **Rumelhart and McClelland modeled past tense as a learned association between present and past sound patterns.** A single trainable network learns across verbs instead of applying a separately specified -ed rule.
The model encodes a root's phonology, transforms that representation through modifiable connections, and decodes an output pattern.
Regularity is a pattern learned from many examples. Irregular forms are also learned within the same system.

title: U-shaped learning
sourceText:
Target phenomena of Rumelhart & McClelland
Because this was one of the first learning models to address a language process, the 
focus was on capturing developmental phenomena.
Specifically: “U-shaped” learning:
- some frequent irregular verbs are learned quite early, e.g., run-ran
- then, spontaneously, children begin producing “regularizations:” runned.
- eventually, they start producing correct forms again.
Learning is “U-shaped” because children often get worse before they get better, so 
performance goes down before it goes back up.
paragraphs: **U-shaped learning describes an initial success, a decline, and later recovery.** A child may correctly say RAN, later produce RUNNED, and eventually return to RAN.
The middle error is a **regularization**, because the child applies the common past-tense pattern to an irregular verb.
The decline does not necessarily mean that the child has stopped learning. A changing system can generalize more broadly while temporarily disrupting an earlier correct response.

title: Words and Rules interpretation of development
sourceText:
Why is U-shaped learning important to the 
“words and rules” approach? 
It’s understood in terms of distinct stages/processes:
- early correct forms are just imitations, don’t depend on the same 
mechanisms as adult processing.
- when the rule is initially learned, it is applied to all cases. We can 
think of the rule as the “best hypothesis” for all items generally.
- over time, exceptions are learned associatively, one-by-one and 
incorporated into lexical knowledge. Further, the “blocking process” 
develops.
paragraphs: **The Words and Rules account explains U-shaped learning through changes in the use of rules and lexical exceptions.** Early correct forms can be imitated before a productive rule is available.
When the rule is learned, it can be applied too broadly, yielding RUNNED. Later, learned irregulars and the blocking process prevent that regularization.
This account treats the developmental stages as involving distinguishable processes rather than only gradual changes in one mapping.

title: U-shaped learning in an associative model
sourceText:
“U-shaped learning” in 
Rumelhart & McClellands’s
model.
- training set is based on data 
about input to children, which 
changes over time.
- Early on, irregular verbs 
predominate – in fact the highest-
frequency verbs tend to have 
irregular past-tense forms: GIVE, 
TAKE, HAVE, GO, etc.
- As the vocabulary expands to 
include more regular forms, the 
model reorganizes to capture those 
regularities.
-- this interferes with some of the 
early-learned forms.
paragraphs: **Changing the training vocabulary can produce U-shaped learning in one network.** Early training emphasizes frequent irregular verbs, allowing those particular mappings to be learned.
As more regular verbs enter training, their common pattern changes the network's responses. That generalization can interfere with previously learned irregulars.
With further learning, the network can recover the irregular responses while retaining broad regularity. No new symbolic rule component is inserted at the point of decline.

title: Testing model generalization
sourceText:
Generalization testing:
The model was trained 
on a small number of 
verbs, so they could 
do a “wug” test with 
real words…
paragraphs: **Testing untrained verbs asks whether the network learned transferable structure.** A real English verb can be novel to a model if it was excluded from that model's training set.
The test therefore uses the logic of a wug task even when the items are real words to humans.
The model can generate many appropriate past-tense features, but feature-level success must be distinguished from producing an entirely correct word.

title: Unusual model outputs
sourceText: But…
paragraphs: **Some model outputs contain changes that are unlike ordinary human regularizations.** Examples include MADE(D)-like changes to MATE and the unusual outputs MEMBLED for MAIL and TOUREDER for TOUR.
The model authors acknowledge that people are unlikely to make some of these errors. They suggest that additional output constraints could reduce bizarre responses.
This separates capturing an overall learning pattern from matching the detailed form of human errors.

title: Phonology and semantics in inflection
sourceText:
A new(er) model: Joanisse & 
Seidenberg (1999)
Theoretical premise:
- “rule-like” generalization is 
supported by phonological 
representations
- “irregular” forms require 
greater support from 
semantics 
Semantics
Speech
Input
Speech
Output
paragraphs: **Joanisse and Seidenberg propose that phonology supports rule-like generalization while semantics especially supports irregular forms.** The same system links speech input, meaning and speech output.
Reliable sound representations support extension from familiar present–past pairs to new forms. Irregular mappings receive additional support from the particular word's semantic representation.
The hypothesis concerns different degrees of dependence on shared systems, rather than a separate symbolic rule route for every regular response.

title: Targeting a neuropsychological dissociation
sourceText:
A new(er) model: Joanisse & 
Seidenberg (1999)
Target phenomenon:
- dissociation between 
irregular and nonword past 
tense in neuropsychological 
data.  
Semantics
Speech
Input
Speech
Output
paragraphs: **The model aims to explain the dissociation between irregular and nonword past-tense performance.** These tasks differ in how much they depend on learned word-specific information and phonological generalization.
A nonword has no familiar item-specific semantic history to support its inflection. A known irregular can require semantic support because its output is not well predicted by the dominant pattern.
Manipulating phonological or semantic integrity tests whether these different dependencies can produce opposite impairment profiles.

title: Broca's aphasia and novel past tense
sourceText:
Neuropsychological data
Broca’s Aphasia
Injury to left anterior brain 
regions
Poor speech production
Problems with regular 
morphology, esp. nonwords
wug wugged, 
blick blicked
paragraphs: **The patient pattern associated here with Broca's aphasia includes especially poor nonword past-tense production.** These patients have left anterior injury and difficulty producing speech.
Regular forms are also vulnerable, while irregular forms are relatively better in the displayed comparison. A novel BLICK must be transformed without relying on a familiar stored past tense.
This motivates investigating phonological contributions to the apparent morphological deficit.

sourceText:
Neuropsychological data: Problems with 
irregulars
Wernicke’s and Alzheimer’s patients
Anomic patients with injury 
to inferior/middle temporal 
brain regions
