paragraphs: **Other patient groups show a larger problem with irregular past-tense forms.** The material discusses Wernicke's and Alzheimer's patients and anomic patients with inferior or middle temporal injury.
Their irregular performance is lower than their regular and nonword performance in the displayed comparison.
This creates the other side of the dissociation and motivates examining the information that especially supports known irregular forms.

title: The classical aphasia contrast
sourceText:
An attractive dichotomy:
Wernicke’s aphasia = “Word salad” or “Jabberwocky,” often with neologisms. Syntax 
roughly intact:
Broca’s aphasia =  “Telegraphic” speech, difficulty with word order and grammatical 
particles (relative sparing of important content words):
paragraphs: **The classical contrast associates Wernicke's aphasia with fluent but often poorly interpretable speech and Broca's aphasia with effortful, telegraphic speech.** The former can include neologisms, while the latter can omit grammatical particles and show word-order difficulty.
This makes a lexical-versus-grammatical interpretation attractive. However, a descriptive syndrome is not itself a demonstration of an isolated processing module.
Content words may be relatively preserved in telegraphic speech, while fluent speech can retain sentence-like structure without conveying a clear message.

title: Historical Broca cases and modern classification
sourceText:
An attractive dichotomy:
Wernicke’s aphasia = problems with activation (inhibition?) in the lexicon.
Broca’s aphasia =  problems with grammar
Note that this is fairly distant from 
how Broca described his original 
cases.
Remember this slide from a few 
weeks ago?
This is confusing: Broca’s actual 
patients would not necessarily be 
classified as Broca’s aphasics. They 
were arguably unable to produce 
speech at all, apparently due to 
motor control issues, and would be 
classified as suffering from apraxia of 
speech.
paragraphs: **Broca's original patients are not necessarily straightforward examples of what is now called Broca's aphasia.** Profound inability to articulate speech can reflect motor-planning impairment rather than a selective grammatical deficit.
**Apraxia of speech** concerns planning or coordinating speech movements. That differs from explaining an omission of grammatical structure in otherwise producible speech.
The historical label therefore should not substitute for a precise description of the impaired behavior.

title: Grammar, lexicon and aphasia
sourceText:
An attractive dichotomy:
Wernicke’s aphasia = problems with activation (inhibition?) in the lexicon.
Broca’s aphasia =  problems with grammar
This dichotomy is interesting in part 
because it seems well aligned with a 
sharp distinction drawn late 20th
Century formal linguistics between 
the grammar and the lexicon.
This starts with Chomsky’s 
formulation of the computational 
problem of language learning, and 
compelling demonstrations of the 
independence of syntax and 
semantics.
paragraphs: **A grammar–lexicon distinction makes the classical aphasia contrast theoretically appealing.** A grammatical system combines forms, while lexical knowledge concerns words and their properties.
Chomsky's example of a grammatical but semantically unusual sentence shows that syntactic well-formedness cannot be reduced to whether a sentence describes a sensible event.
That conceptual distinction does not establish a simple one-to-one mapping from each syndrome to one isolated component.

title: Levels of speech production
sourceText:
An attractive dichotomy:
Wernicke’s aphasia = problems with activation (inhibition?) in the lexicon.
Broca’s aphasia =  problems with grammar
Consider, too, the difference between 
the Functional and Positional levels in 
our speech production model.
Lemmas have an arbitrary relationship 
to their referents. 
But the syntactic trees, affixes, etc. at 
the positional level are the product of 
abstract syntactic processes.
“But,” you might object “what about 
words like HOUSEBOAT and DOGHOUSE, 
where the meaning is clearly not 
arbitrary,” and I would remind you of 
speech error evidence that derivational 
morphology is done at the positional 
level, e.g., easy enoughly.
paragraphs: **The functional level selects word meanings and semantic roles, while the positional level organizes word forms into a grammatical sequence.** Phonological encoding and articulation concern later aspects of producing the utterance.
A **lemma** is a representation involved in lexical selection, distinct from simply executing its sound pattern. Positional processing contributes ordering and morphological structure.
Combinations such as HOUSEBOAT show that complex-word meaning can be partly compositional. Errors such as “easy enoughly” provide evidence about the organization of morphological operations.

title: Egocentric and absolute spatial language
sourceText:
Thinking about space…
It seems natural in most languages to talk 
about space egocentrically when talking about 
things that are nearby.
What is to your left or to your right, in front of 
you or behind you, etc.
Not so in Tzeltal, a Western Mayan language 
spoken in Chiapas.
In this language (and a small number of others, 
mostly unrelated to one another, and broadly 
distributed, e.g., in Bali and Queensland) 
absolute directions are used.
Raise your east hand if this seems intuitive to 
you… 
Some native Tzeltal speakers defending their land 
from the vampire squid of neoliberalism.
paragraphs: **Egocentric spatial descriptions use the speaker's position and orientation.** Left, right, in front and behind are familiar examples for nearby objects.
Tzeltal commonly uses absolute directions in circumstances where English speakers might use these relative terms.
The contrast motivates asking whether habitual language use relates to nonverbal spatial coding, rather than merely comparing two ways of giving spoken directions.

title: Tzeltal uphill and downhill
sourceText:
Tzeltal has a historically landmark-
based system.
Things are either “uphill” or 
“downhill” from one another, not to 
the left or right of the speaker or 
interlocutor.
In fact, “uphill” and “downhill” are 
used as cardinal directions, making 
this an absolute system. 
Beautiful downtown Tenejapa.
(Levinson et al., 2002, Cognition)
paragraphs: **Tzeltal's uphill and downhill terms function as an absolute directional system.** Their historical connection to a slope does not mean that each use simply points to the nearest visible hill.
A direction is retained as a stable spatial reference rather than being recalculated from the speaker's current left and right.
This allows positions to be described consistently as the speaker changes orientation.

title: The rotated spatial-memory task
sourceText:
Majid et al. (2004, TiCS)
A non-linguistic test for relative vs. absolute coding of space
paragraphs: **The chips task separates relative from absolute spatial memory by rotating the participant 180 degrees.** A participant sees a configuration, waits, and then chooses its match at a second table.
A relative response preserves the arrangement with respect to the person's viewpoint. An absolute response preserves its orientation in the environment, so the two responses diverge after rotation.

Dutch speakers predominantly gave relative responses, while Tzeltal speakers gave more absolute responses. The association is consistent with their preferred linguistic frames but does not isolate language from all other experience.

title: Spatial inference across displays
sourceText:
Majid et al. (2004, TiCS)
You can get really fancy with this.
paragraphs: **Spatial inference can combine relations learned in different displays.** Participants learn the relation between two objects, rotate to another display, and learn a second relation involving a shared object.
They then place an object relative to another using the combined information. Relative and absolute coding lead to different placements because the person's orientation has changed.
Dutch and Tzeltal response patterns again differ in the direction associated with their preferred spatial frames.

title: A testing-environment alternative
sourceText:
Li and Gleitman:
Inducing landmark-based similarity in English speakers 
Consider the conditions under which 
the Tzeltal speakers were tested: 
Outside, with visible, familiar landmarks. 
Typical psychology lab studies are done 
in windowless rooms.
paragraphs: **Testing conditions could contribute to the apparent language-group difference.** Li and Gleitman noted that Tzeltal participants had been tested with visible, familiar outdoor landmarks, unlike many laboratory participants.
An environment with useful landmarks can encourage landmark-based coding. A windowless laboratory can make viewer-relative descriptions more convenient.
Manipulating landmark availability within English speakers tests whether the behavior can change without changing native language.

title: Blinds down, blinds up and outdoors
sourceText:
In the “blinds down” condition, English 
speakers overwhelmingly use relative position 
in this task – like the Dutch speakers in prior 
studies.
With the blinds up and a view of the street, or 
outdoors, their preference is less pronounced. 
Li and Gleitman:
Inducing landmark-based spatial reasoning in English 
speakers
paragraphs: **English speakers' preference for relative coding weakened when external landmarks were available.** They strongly preferred relative responses with the blinds down, but the preference was less pronounced with a street view or outdoors.
The manipulation changes the spatial information available while keeping the language group the same.
This demonstrates that task context can influence the response. It challenges an explanation in which language alone fixes the chosen frame.

title: Levinson's methodological response
sourceText:
Levinson and colleagues 
were not impressed.
They claim that Li and 
Gleitman made it too 
transparent that they were 
testing something to do 
with rotation by reducing 
memory load and 
time/distance between 
stimulus and test.
Also Li and Gleitman’s
participants were Ivy 
League students, who excel 
at figuring out what the 
professor wants and then 
making it happen.
paragraphs: **Levinson and colleagues argued that the simplified task could make the experimenter's purpose too obvious.** Low memory demands and short time or distance between displays may encourage a deliberate strategy about rotation.
Participants who infer what is being tested can alter their response for reasons different from habitual spatial coding.
The response therefore focuses on memory load and task transparency, rather than denying that landmarks can ever matter.

title: Testing categorical perception in sign
sourceText: Research question: Is there categorical perception for these dimensions?
paragraphs: **Categorical perception can be tested by varying a sign feature continuously.** The hand-configuration continuum moves between forms while the observer's identification and discrimination responses are measured.
One continuum crosses a phonemic distinction between PLEASE and SORRY. The allophonic comparison varies hand configuration without the same change in sign identity.
A sharp identification boundary accompanied by better discrimination near that boundary would indicate category-sensitive perception.

title: Identification and discrimination results
sourceText:
These curves should look 
familiar.
There is a fairly sharp 
categorical boundary between 
stimuli 4 and 6 for the 
phonemic boundary. 
This corresponds to the peak in 
the discrimination function.
For the allophonic condition, 
the identification function is 
much shallower – i.e., many 
more ambiguous stimuli – and 
there is no peak in the 
discrimination function.
paragraphs: **Deaf signers show a sharper categorical boundary for phonemic than allophonic hand-configuration changes.** In the phonemic condition, identification shifts steeply around stimuli 4–6.
Discrimination is also strongest near the phonemic boundary. Comparable physical steps are easier to distinguish when they cross that category boundary.
The allophonic identification function is shallower and lacks the same localized discrimination peak. This links the perceptual pattern to linguistic contrast rather than any visible hand change.

title: Shared and modality-related brain activity
sourceText:
Brain activity during sign language comprehension has both important 
similarities and differences with spoken language.
Similar: 
- left lateralization
- classical language areas 
(Broca’s / inferior frontal; Wernicke’s
/ posterior superior temporal)
Different:
- +visual areas (-auditory areas)
- superior parietal / classic 
spatial areas
Campbell, MacSweeney, & Waters (2008)
Deaf signers
Hearing signers
Audio-visual 
Speech (hearing participants)
paragraphs: **Signed-language comprehension recruits classical language regions and shows left lateralization, as spoken-language comprehension does.** Inferior frontal and posterior superior temporal regions are part of this overlap.
Signing also engages visual and superior parietal regions relevant to its perceptual and spatial demands.
The combination suggests both common language organization and modality-related contributions. Similarity does not require identical activation everywhere.

title: Evidence about signed language
sourceText:
So, sign language…
Sign language has phonological structure, and native speakers show categorical perception 
for some contrastive features.
Learning a signed language results in some brain reorganization, particularly the 
lateralization of motion processing.
Although attention to the visual periphery is critical for both hearing and deaf signers, only 
deaf signers show enhanced processing of visual attention in the periphery.
Compared with non-language stimuli that also involve organized, sequenced hand 
movements, signed sentences activate posterior STG (Wernicke’s area).
paragraphs: **Signed languages have linguistic form, grammar and language-related neural organization.** Contrastive sign features can produce categorical perception, and comprehension recruits posterior superior temporal language regions.
Signing experience is associated with changes in motion lateralization. Deafness is associated with enhanced peripheral attention in the reported comparison.
These findings jointly show that linguistic experience and sensory history contribute in different ways.

title: Exercise and maturational-state hypotheses
sourceText:
Two versions of the “critical period” hypothesis
Which of these do you think JN89 see as more consistent with their data?
Does this change our interpretation of the L1 critical period data?
paragraphs: **The exercise hypothesis proposes that early language use preserves language-learning capacity, while the maturational-state hypothesis allows capacity to decline despite early use.** Both assume an early advantage, but they differ in what early successful experience protects.
Later second-language difficulty in people who already acquired a first language is more directly compatible with maturation than with complete preservation through exercise.
This does not make early first-language experience unimportant. Early access and age-related change address related but distinct questions.

title: Early language access and later learning
sourceText:
Mayberry, Lock, & Kazmi (2002, Nature)
Many deaf children do not get sign language input, 
but have an otherwise typical upbringing.
Children (ages 9-15) have difficulty learning 
American Sign Language (ASL) if this is their first time 
learning a language.
A comparison group of children who went deaf after 
initially learning a spoken language do much better.
These differences persist into adulthood.
paragraphs: **Mayberry, Lock and Kazmi compared later language learning after different early-language histories.** Deaf individuals without accessible early language performed worse than those who had acquired an early spoken or signed language.

Children first exposed to ASL at ages 9–15 had particular difficulty when it was also their first language. Those who had first learned a spoken language did much better, and the differences persisted.
The comparison distinguishes late first-language learning from late acquisition of an additional language.

title: Controlling visual similarity in blocking
sourceText:
Dealing with potential confounds 101
What if the blocking effect arises at the level of 
visual object recognition?
Two responses:
1. Stimuli were normed so that objects in 
the same category were not more visually 
similar to one another than objects in different 
categories, on average.
2.  A control experiment was run in which 
visual similarity was blocked along, and 
different results were found.
Specifically, the blocking effect was 
observed in the first block of trials. 
Thus, the effects in Experiment 1 aren’t likely 
to be due to visual similarity.
paragraphs: **Semantic blocking effects must be separated from visual-recognition difficulty.** Objects from one semantic category could resemble one another visually, creating a potential confound in naming.
The materials were normed so that same-category items were not more visually similar on average. A separate visual-similarity manipulation also produced a different time course.
Visual blocking affected the first block, whereas the semantic pattern of interest developed differently. This weakens a purely visual explanation.

title: Simultaneous displays and serial naming
sourceText:
Yeah, but what about that Hermens et al., study, where people saw multiple 
objects simultaneously, and they didn’t find an effect?
Maybe there’s just something weird about seeing objects in serial?
Belke et al. address this by asking participants to view displays of four items 
simultaneously and produce their names in serial.
paragraphs: **Belke and colleagues presented four objects simultaneously but required their names in sequence.** This tests whether the absence of an effect in another simultaneous-display study depended on presentation format.
Displaying all objects at once reduces dependence on a succession of isolated pictures. Serial naming still requires selecting and producing one label after another.
Eye tracking provides additional timing information about the processing of each object.

title: Gaze duration and eye–speech lag
sourceText: They measure eye-movements while they do this.
paragraphs: **Eye movements and speech onsets provide different timing measures during serial naming.** Gaze duration records how long the eyes remain on an object, while eye–speech lag concerns the interval between leaving it and beginning its spoken name.
A participant can move the eyes toward the next object before articulating the current one. The measures therefore separate overlapping parts of preparation.
Different blocking effects on these measures can help constrain the processing stage affected.

title: Where the blocking effect appears
sourceText:
Overall duration of speech 
decreases over the course of 
the experiment, but doesn’t 
show a blocking effect.
gesture level
Gaze duration shows a 
blocking effect, but only after 
the first cycle.
lemma selection
There’s no effect on lag. 
Numerically, the blocking 
effect seems to go in the 
opposite direction, but this is 
not significant.
phonological encoding
paragraphs: **Semantic blocking increases gaze duration after the first presentation cycle, but not overall speech duration or eye–speech lag.** The measures therefore do not show a uniform slowdown.
Speech duration decreases with repetition without a blocking difference. Gaze duration shows the condition difference after the first cycle.

The nonsignificant lag difference should not be reported as evidence for a reversed effect. The reported pattern is interpreted as supporting a contribution at lemma selection rather than articulation or phonological encoding.

title: Thresholded or cascaded speech processing?
sourceText:
So, we want to know, is phoneme identification for word recognition more like thresholded
(lumber mill) or cascaded (food web) processing?
McMurray, B., Tanenhaus, M., Aslin, R. and Spivey, M. (2003). 
Probabilistic constraint satisfaction at the lexical/phonetic interface: 
Evidence for gradient effects of within-category VOT on lexical 
access. Journal of Psycholinguistic Research, 32, 77-97.
http://www2.psychology.uiowa.edu/faculty/mcmurray/publications/
mcmurray-jpr.pdf 
McMurray et al. tested identification of a /b/-/p/ 
continuum in a “visual world” display for eye-
tracking.
paragraphs: **McMurray and colleagues tested whether fine phonetic information affects lexical competition.** Participants heard a /b/–/p/ continuum while viewing pictures including BEAR and PEAR, with eye movements recorded.
**Voice onset time**, or VOT, varies the timing between release and voicing. It can change how strongly the sound supports /b/ or /p/.
A thresholded account would pass a completed categorical decision onward. A cascaded account allows graded information to influence word candidates before uncertainty is fully resolved.

title: Categorical mouse choices
sourceText:
So, we want to know, is phoneme identification for word recognition more like thresholded
(lumber mill) or cascaded (food web) processing?
Participants used the mouse to select the 
picture most consistent with what they 
heard, e.g., a “bear” or a “pear,” just like 
in the experiment you did at home.
A typical, step-like, identification function 
was observed.
paragraphs: **Participants selected the picture that best matched the spoken item.** Their BEAR–PEAR choices produced a typical step-like identification function across VOT.
Shorter VOTs favored the /b/ response and longer VOTs the /p/ response. Near the boundary, the preferred category changed rapidly.
A categorical-looking final response does not establish that all earlier lexical activation was categorical.

title: Graded lexical competition
sourceText:
Eye-movements reveal that ambiguity is gradient, i.e., there are more looks to the competitor 
close to the boundary.
paragraphs: **Competitor looks vary with phonetic ambiguity even within a chosen category.** Tokens closer to the /b/–/p/ boundary produce more competition than clear tokens farther from it.
A participant can ultimately select BEAR while spending more time looking at PEAR when the sound is close to the boundary.
This supports the claim that fine phonetic information remains relevant to lexical activation, rather than disappearing completely after a categorical phoneme decision.

title: Distance from the boundary and time
sourceText: The effect is a lot clearer viewed this way…
paragraphs: **Competitor fixation increases as a token approaches the category boundary from either side.** For BEAR responses, more /p/-like VOT increases looks to PEAR. For PEAR responses, more /b/-like VOT increases looks to BEAR.
The graph separates early and late observation windows. The gradient remains visible in the later competition measure, supporting continued sensitivity to within-category phonetic detail.
The result favors cascaded use of graded evidence over a model that transmits only a completed phoneme label with all within-category detail discarded.
